The Three Friends In the past year, I’ve helped advised three friends build their GP tech stacks from scratch.
Maybe it’s my network. Or maybe AI is democratizing operational knowledge in real time. The data suggests the latter: small businesses closed a technology gap with enterprises in 18 months that previously took decades. In February 2024, large businesses used AI at 1.8x the rate of small businesses. By August 2025, that gap had nearly vanished.1
What I learned from those three conversations shapes everything I’d recommend today.
The first friend was paralyzed by fear of the unknown. He’d never built a tech stack before—always inherited whatever the previous operator used. The beautiful irony? He used Claude and ChatGPT to educate himself through the process. AI became his tutor before it became his tool.
But here’s the caveat I had to drill into him: AI tends to tell you what you want to hear. It’s sycophantic by design. And it hallucinates. He learned to treat AI like a smart intern—capable, but requiring verification. Never an oracle.
The second friend got burned by API pricing. She chose a vendor, built integrations, got everything humming—then got hit with unexpected API usage charges. Lesson learned: with MCP adoption growing, expect vendors to monetize API access. The cost of “free” APIs rarely stays free. Ask about pricing upfront. Get it in writing.
The third friend was trapped. Already invested in a legacy system, she hesitated to change vendors because of the integration nightmare she’d face. The sunk cost fallacy plus switching cost fear equals paralysis. But here’s the truth: the longer you wait, the more painful migration becomes. Build on open rails from day one.
Three friends. Three lessons. One conclusion: the technical stack you choose today determines whether AI becomes your leverage—or your limitation.
The Old Stack Problem The traditional CRE tech stack was built for data entry, not intelligence.
You know the workflow: Click through screens. Export to Excel. Email PDFs. Repeat.
Integration meant six-figure consulting projects. Data lived in silos. And the reports? Unlike some legacy vendors that still have a default Excel output with blank rows, different merged cells across headers and records, and internal hyperlinks that break the moment you try to automate.
If you know, you know.
The old stack was designed for a world where humans did the thinking and software did the storing. That world is ending.
The Turning Point: Conversation as Interface MCP and AI agents change the game.
For the first time, you can build a stack where an AI assistant orchestrates across systems—pull loan covenants, check construction draws against budget, draft capital call notices—all through conversation.
The interface isn’t a dashboard anymore. It’s a question.
“What’s our debt service coverage ratio covenant on the Main Street property?”
“Are we over budget on electrical for the Phase 2 development?”
“Draft a capital call notice for Q1—$2.4M total, pro-rata across the LP base.”
This isn’t science fiction. This is what Claude Projects, ChatGPT Enterprise, and Gemini for Workspace enable today. The infrastructure exists. The question is whether your stack is ready to plug into it.
The Stack: Four Principles I don’t believe in prescribing exact vendors. Markets change. Features evolve. What matters are the principles.
1. Start with the Brain: Data Warehouse as Foundation Snowflake or Databricks as the single source of truth.
Why? All roads lead here. Every system feeds the warehouse; every insight pulls from it. The warehouse enables AI agents to reason across your entire operation—not just one property, one fund, one workflow.
When someone asks “How are we performing across the portfolio?” the answer shouldn’t require three exports and a pivot table. It should be a query.
The startup caveat: If you’re a smaller GP or just starting out, you don’t need a data warehouse on day one. AI agents can pull data just-in-time via APIs—query your accounting system directly, fetch from your property management platform as needed. The decision point comes as you scale: more properties, more funds, more complex cross-portfolio questions. At some point, I don’t see how you live without a centralized data layer. But don’t over-engineer before you have the complexity to justify it.
2. Choose Pipes, Not Walls: Open API as Non-Negotiable I’d strongly consider walking away from any vendor without open APIs.
Open APIs aren’t a feature—they’re a philosophy. Closed ecosystems mean expensive integrations mean your data held hostage. The vendor that won’t let you export is the vendor betting you’ll never leave.
Evaluation criteria:
API documentation quality (is it comprehensive or an afterthought?) API pricing model (per-call vs. unlimited) Data export capabilities (avoid the merged-cell Excel nightmare) Integration ecosystem (who else has connected?) 3. Build for Agents: MCP-Ready Partners I’d prioritize vendors with MCP servers or clear API documentation that would support one.
Why? MCP (Model Context Protocol) is emerging as the standard for how AI agents connect to data sources. Think of it like USB for AI—a universal plug. Vendors who support it reduce your integration costs to near-zero. Vendors who don’t will require custom middleware.
The best integration is no integration.
As MCP adoption grows, expect this to become table stakes. Early movers get cleaner architectures. Late movers get technical debt.
4. Center on Conversation: Chat Apps as the Operational Layer Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini as the primary interface—not just a chatbot, but the orchestration layer.
Canvas and Artifacts for ad-hoc reporting. Projects for organizing deal-specific context. Skills for consistent document generation.
Your next analyst won’t need a desk.
The operator’s workflow shifts from clicking to asking. From navigating menus to describing intent. From waiting for reports to conversing with data.
The Stack by Function Here’s how I’d map it:
Function Approach Notes Productivity O365 or Google Suite + Slack O365 if Excel is non-negotiable Corporate Accounting QuickBooks, Ramp Ramp for expense automation Asset-Level Systems DoorLoop, AppFolio, Re-Leased, Entrata Newer generation; avoid legacy Data Warehouse Snowflake, Databricks The brain—all data flows here Ad-Hoc Reporting Claude Canvas, ChatGPT Artifacts Conversation-driven analysis Dashboards Hex, Mode Modern, code-friendly BI Orchestration Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini MCP servers as the glue On asset-level systems specifically: the market has options now. DoorLoop ranks highest for commercial property management. AppFolio leads in AI-powered automation. Re-Leased is purpose-built for commercial and mixed-use. Entrata handles enterprise-grade complexity. MRI Software unifies the full suite.
The key isn’t which one you pick—it’s verifying they meet the principles: open API, clean exports, integration-ready.
Enterprise AI: Choosing Your Orchestration Layer The chat apps aren’t equal. Here’s how they differ for GP workflows:
ChatGPT Teams/Enterprise Projects: Files, instructions, and chats in one place; memory isolation between projects Connectors: Pull from Google Drive, SharePoint, GitHub, Microsoft Teams, Gmail Admin controls: Role-based permissions, SOC 2, ISO 27001 certified Best for: Teams already deep in Microsoft/Google ecosystems who want broad connectivity Claude Teams/Enterprise 500K token context window (2x standard)—can ingest entire lease agreements Projects: Upload files to create deal-specific AI assistants Memory (2025): Learns team processes, client needs, project details Claude Code: Agentic coding for building automations Best for: Complex document analysis, custom skill development, technical teams Gemini Enterprise (Google Workspace) Native integration: Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive, Meet Cross-platform: Also connects to Microsoft 365, Salesforce, SAP NotebookLM Plus: Mind maps, research synthesis Deep Research: Agentic search with source citations Best for: Google-native shops, O365/Google hybrid environments Choose based on where your data already lives and where your team already works.
GP Workflows: What This Actually Looks Like Here’s how “conversation as interface” applies to real GP operations:
Workflow How AI Chat Apps Help Loan Document Management Upload loan docs, covenants, amendments to a Project. Ask “What’s our DSCR covenant?” or “When is the next interest rate reset?” Monthly Cash Forecasting Generate cash flow models from bank feeds + lease schedules using Canvas/Artifacts. Iterate in conversation. Capital Call Letters Use Skills/Custom GPTs for consistent formatting. Auto-populate investor details, calculate pro-rata amounts. Development Budget Tracking Upload draw schedules, invoices, change orders. Ask “Are we over budget on electrical?” Investor Reporting Pull from property management + accounting via connectors. Generate quarterly reports with consistent tone. Meeting Notes → Actions Summarize meetings, extract action items, push to task management. The best software isn’t the one with the most features—it’s the one you can talk to.
The Architecture Here’s how it fits together:
The conversation layer sits on top. The data layer unifies everything. The operational systems feed in through APIs. Reports flow out through the tools that match the use case.
Bidirectional. Open. Queryable.
The SME Advantage Here’s what the data says:
91% of AI-using SMBs report revenue lift2 86% report improved profit margins AI acts as a “force multiplier”—small teams achieve the capacity of much larger enterprises3 Companies with 10-100 employees saw AI usage jump from 47% to 68% year-over-year4 Meanwhile, enterprises are stuck. 80% set efficiency and cost-cutting as their primary AI objective.5 Budgets remained constrained. AI stayed in “experimental” mode.
Enterprises are using AI to cut costs. The smartest small operators are using it to build capacity they could never afford.
The GP that builds this stack today isn’t just choosing software. They’re betting on a future where operational leverage comes from intelligence, not headcount.
The Honest Caveat I’d be doing you a disservice if I didn’t repeat this: AI tools are powerful but imperfect.
Sycophancy: These models tend to tell you what you want to hear. If you ask “Is this a good deal?” they’ll find reasons to say yes. Set expectations with your team: verify, don’t trust blindly.
Hallucination: AI fabricates facts and research. Always verify critical information—especially numbers, dates, and legal language.
The meta-beauty: You can use AI to learn how to build your stack (my first friend did exactly this). But treat it as a smart intern, not an oracle. The quality of output depends entirely on the quality of your verification.
Starting Today Three questions to ask yourself:
What data do we have that’s underutilized because it’s hard to access? That’s your MCP opportunity.
What expertise exists in someone’s head that should be captured as a reusable skill? That’s your Skills opportunity.
What repetitive analysis could we turn into a conversational question? That’s your Prompts opportunity.
The tools are here. The infrastructure is ready.
I’d love to hear what’s working for you. What does your stack look like? What vendors have surprised you—for better or worse? Drop a comment or reach out.
Build on open rails from day one.
These are my personal opinions based on experience helping friends and colleagues. Your mileage may vary—every GP’s needs are different. I have no financial relationship with any vendors mentioned.

The Three-Hour Clone In March 2025, Manus AI launched with a demo video that racked up 200,000 views in 24 hours. Within a week, two million people had joined the waitlist. Invitation codes were reselling for up to $13,500. Jack Dorsey called it “excellent.” Economists were declaring it “ahead of its American counterparts.”
Eight months later, the company announced it had hit $100 million in annual recurring revenue—the fastest journey from zero to $100M ARR in startup history.
Here’s the twist: within three hours of launch, the MetaGPT team had replicated Manus’s core functionality in an open-source project called OpenManus. It quickly garnered over 23,000 GitHub stars.
The fastest-growing AI company in history was cloned in three hours. That’s not a bug—it’s a feature.
This paradox tells us something important about where we actually are with autonomous AI agents—and where value will accrue as this space matures. If you’re a product manager, executive, or anyone evaluating agentic AI for your organization, the Manus story offers three critical lessons about what matters and what doesn’t.
The Wrapper Wars “Extreme repackaging.”
That’s how CEO Xiao Hong describes what Manus does. He calls it “kitbashing”—a model-building term for combining existing parts into something new. Critics use harsher language: they say Manus is “essentially repackaging existing technologies rather than introducing novel solutions.”
The technical reality supports both views. Under the hood, Manus dynamically invokes Anthropic’s Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet and fine-tuned versions of Alibaba’s Qwen. It doesn’t train its own foundation models. It orchestrates existing ones.
This triggered what I’ve started calling the Wrapper Wars—a debate that’s now playing out across the AI industry. Is orchestration valuable, or is it just plumbing? Should companies build their own AI capabilities, buy platforms like Manus, or wait for the inevitable commoditization?
For product managers, this debate feels familiar. It’s the classic build-vs-buy decision, but with higher stakes and faster timelines. And it connects directly to something I’ve been thinking about since writing about AI hallucinations: if Manus uses Claude / Qwen underneath, it inherits their limitations. The ground level hallucination rate doesn’t disappear because you’ve wrapped it in a pretty interface.
So why is Manus still growing?
What OpenManus Got Wrong OpenManus proved an important point: the models aren’t the moat. You can replicate the concept of an autonomous agent calling Claude and browsing the web in a weekend hackathon.
But there’s a gap between replicating a concept and building a production system. And that gap is where the real work—and the real value—lives.
Manus’s architecture involves five specialized sub-agents working in concert: a Planning Agent for generating task chains, an Information Retrieval Agent for knowledge gathering, a Code Generation Agent, a Tool Execution Agent managing browser and shell operations, and a Verification Agent implementing dual-verification for reliability. These agents operate within an isolated Ubuntu Linux sandbox, averaging 50 tool calls per task.
The key innovation isn’t calling Claude. It’s the CodeAct paradigm—generating executable Python scripts that can flexibly combine tools, implement conditional logic, and self-debug iteratively. This is based on 2024 research showing that executable code outperforms fixed JSON tool templates for agent actions.
It’s the difference between a prototype and a production line. OpenManus showed that anyone can build a prototype. Manus showed that turning a prototype into a product that handles edge cases, manages errors gracefully, and scales to 147 trillion tokens processed—that’s where the engineering challenge actually lies.
This mirrors something I wrote about in my post on context engineering: the bottleneck is context, not code. In agentic AI, the corollary is clear: the bottleneck is orchestration, not models.
Three Lessons from the Manus Story Consumer UX Beats Raw Capability While OpenAI’s Operator emphasizes precision with human confirmations and Anthropic’s Computer Use targets developers through APIs, Manus made a different bet: go consumer-first with an intuitive, fully autonomous experience.
The result is “Manus’s Computer”—a transparent interface where users watch the agent work in real-time, seeing browser activity, terminal commands, and code edits simultaneously. Sessions are replayable. Tasks continue asynchronously even when you close your laptop. One-click deployment can build and host full-stack applications.
Xiao Hong put it simply: “The most powerful AI is the one that actually gets used. Not the one with the best model, but the one that fits into your life.”
This is the same lesson we’ve learned repeatedly in enterprise software. Features don’t win—usability does. The best technology that sits unused loses to the “good enough” technology that becomes habitual. Brazil, surprisingly, comprises 33% of Manus’s user base—not because Brazilians have better AI infrastructure, but because the product actually works for their workflows.
The Moat Is in the Plumbing If OpenManus can replicate the concept in three hours, where’s the defensibility?
It’s in the boring parts. The 29+ specialized tool integrations spanning browser control, shell execution, file management, and third-party APIs. The error handling that prevents infinite loops. The retry logic that recovers from failures. The verification agent that catches mistakes before they compound.
Every production AI system I’ve seen follows the same pattern: 20% of the effort goes into the “AI” part, and 80% goes into the infrastructure that makes it reliable. The orchestration layer—the “plumbing”—is where months of engineering accumulate into competitive advantage.
This connects directly to my earlier writing on context engineering. Just as the bottleneck in knowledge work isn’t analysis but context management, the bottleneck in agentic AI isn’t the model but the orchestration. The wrapper isn’t a limitation—it’s the product.
Pricing Signals Commoditization Manus costs roughly $2 per task—approximately one-tenth the price of comparable OpenAI offerings. The free tier offers 300 daily credits. Starter plans run $39/month.
This aggressive pricing tells us something important: the orchestration layer is commoditizing faster than anyone expected. If Manus can profitably offer 10x cheaper pricing, it means the underlying costs (API calls to Claude and Qwen, compute for sandboxes) are dropping rapidly. And if orchestration commoditizes, what’s left?
When the technology commoditizes, the wrapper becomes the product. Brand, trust, integrations, and user experience become the differentiators. This is why Manus invested heavily in Discord community building (138,000+ members), regional expansion (Japan, Middle East, Brazil), and ecosystem integrations (Google Drive Connector, Nano Banana Pro for slides).
The race isn’t for better models. It’s for better distribution.
The Intelligent Intern Problem Before anyone gets too excited, let’s talk about what Manus actually is—and isn’t.
MIT Technology Review’s hands-on testing positioned it as “a highly intelligent and efficient intern.” TechCrunch’s Kyle Wiggers described initial performance as “disappointing,” noting struggles with “consistent accuracy and deeper analytical tasks.” Users report infinite loops, error messages, and system freezes. The team acknowledges relatively high failure rates compared to simpler systems like ChatGPT.
The GAIA benchmark scores look impressive (86.5% on Level 1 tasks), but real-world testing reveals performance gaps. MIT found the system sometimes “got lazy” and took shortcuts on complex analytical tasks.
This matters for enterprise adoption. Manus works well for research synthesis, data visualization, travel planning, and prototyping—tasks where occasional errors are acceptable and human review is expected. It’s not ready for mission-critical applications where reliability matters more than speed.
The “intelligent intern” framing is apt. You wouldn’t give an intern unsupervised access to customer communications or financial transactions. The same logic applies to current agentic AI systems.
The Real Moat The Manus story reveals where value actually accrues in the agentic AI era—and it’s not where most people are looking.
Models are commoditizing. Meta releases Llama, Alibaba releases Qwen, and Google and OpenAI race to the bottom on API pricing. The foundation layer is becoming table stakes.
Orchestration is commoditizing too, but slower. OpenManus proved the concept is replicable; Manus proved the production version requires substantial engineering. This is where companies can still build temporary competitive advantages.
What remains? Distribution, brand, and trust. Manus’s Discord community, regional expansion, and ecosystem integrations aren’t afterthoughts—they’re the strategy. When the technology commoditizes, relationships become the moat.
This mirrors the lesson from my previous posts on context engineering. I wrote that “the bottleneck is context, not code”—that in knowledge work, the value isn’t in generating ideas but in managing information flow, aligning stakeholders, and building systems that surface the right context at the right time.
In agentic AI, the parallel is clear. The value isn’t in the model. It’s in the orchestration that makes the model useful, the UX that makes it accessible, and the trust that makes enterprises willing to adopt it.
In the age of commoditized intelligence, execution becomes everything.
What This Means for You If you’re evaluating agentic AI for your organization, the Manus story offers practical guidance:
Don’t wait for perfect. Current systems are “intelligent interns,” not autonomous experts. Use them for intern-appropriate tasks: research, data synthesis, prototyping, first drafts.
Evaluate orchestration, not models. When comparing platforms, ask about error handling, retry logic, and verification systems. The “AI” is increasingly commoditized; the plumbing differentiates.
Plan for commoditization. Whatever advantage you build today will erode. Focus on proprietary data, workflow integration, and user adoption—the parts that compound over time.
Watch the pricing signals. Manus at $2/task tells you that OpenAI at $20/task will face pressure. Build your cost models accordingly.
The Manus paradox—fastest growth, fastest clone—isn’t a contradiction. It’s a preview of how the entire AI market will evolve. The models commoditize. The orchestration commoditizes more slowly. And the human elements—design, trust, relationships—become exponentially more valuable.
Same lesson as always. The bottleneck is never where you think it is.

The Paradox I just shipped an iOS app. It helps runners get AI-powered analysis of their workouts and generate shareable art from their stats.
But the app itself has no AI.
No GPT integration. No on-device model. No API calls to Claude or Gemini. Zero intelligence inside.
And that’s exactly why it works.
The Backstory Last month, I replaced $200/year in fitness subscriptions with a weekend project — an AI system that gave me personalized coaching by connecting Claude to my running database. (That story here.)
At the end, I wrote: “I’m exploring building this into an iOS app.”
Two Saturdays later, I did. 98% AI-generated code. Zero AI inside.
What the App Actually Does The app has two core features:
1. Export .fit Files for Analysis The app reads your workouts from Apple Health and exports them as .fit files — a universal workout format that Garmin, Strava, and other fitness platforms understand. You can then share these files directly to Claude (or any AI), where my custom running analysis prompt turns raw data into personalized coaching.
The app’s role: Extract context from Apple Health.
Claude’s role: Apply expertise and generate insights.
2. Generate Art Prompts for Sharing Choose an art style — Ghibli, HD-2D pixel art, Chinese 古风, isometric cityscape — and the app constructs an image generation prompt using your run stats (distance, pace, heart rate, location).
Then you pick your AI: Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, or just copy the prompt.
The app’s role: Build the prompt with your data.
You decide: Which AI generates the image.
Why No AI Inside? Here’s the mental model that changed how I think about building apps:
The Old Model: App = The Experience Traditional apps try to own everything — the UI, the intelligence, the insights. Data flows into the app. Users live inside the app.
If you wanted AI features, you’d integrate OpenAI’s API, pay per token, handle rate limits, build fallbacks.
The New Model: App = Context Exporter My app doesn’t try to be smart. It tries to be useful to smart things.
For analysis: It exports .fit files so Claude can do the heavy lifting. For art: It exports prompts so users can choose their preferred AI. The app is a context bridge — it liberates data trapped in Apple Health and packages it for AI consumption.
Don’t wrap AI. Export context.
“Why Not Just Connect Claude Directly?” Fair question. There are tools that let AI assistants connect directly to your data — databases, cloud documents, that kind of thing. So why build an app at all?
Because your health data is locked on your phone.
Most of your digital life lives in the cloud, accessible through APIs. But Apple Health is different:
Your workout data lives locally on your iPhone Apple doesn’t let external tools access it directly You need an iOS app to unlock that data Think of it this way: AI can read files you share with it, but it can’t reach into your pocket and grab your phone.
My app is the bridge. It extracts the data Apple protects, packages it in a format AI understands, and hands it off. The AI does the thinking. The app does the unlocking.
The Vibe Coding Experience Let’s talk about how I actually built this.
Tools used: Claude Code (Anthropic’s agentic coding tool)
Time: Two Saturdays
AI-generated code: ~98%
I’m not a Swift developer. I’d never built an iOS app before. But Claude Code handled:
All the visual design and screen layouts Connecting to Apple Health and reading workout data Converting workouts to the .fit format Building the art prompt generator The “share to…” functionality All six art style themes My job was:
Describing what I wanted Testing on device Steering when things went wrong Making product decisions The vibe coding reality: I’d describe a feature, Claude would generate it, I’d test it, we’d iterate. Most of the time, it just worked. When it didn’t, I’d paste the error and Claude would fix it.
The frustrating part: Apple’s App Store review. My first submission got rejected — they wanted more explanation of how the app uses health data. Fair enough. But it meant rewriting privacy descriptions, waiting for re-review, and refreshing my email for days. The AI couldn’t help with that.
The moment I knew vibe coding was real: I described the art prompt feature in two sentences, and Claude generated a working style picker with six themes in under a minute. I’d budgeted half a day for that feature.
This isn’t “AI wrote my app for me.” It’s more like pair programming with a very fast, very patient partner who knows every API but needs guidance on product direction.
What This Means for Builders There’s a whole category of “context bridge” apps waiting to be built:
Bank transaction exporters for budget analysis Calendar context for meeting prep Health data aggregators for wellness coaching Code context exporters for review and debugging The intelligence layer is becoming commoditized. The context layer is the new moat.
Try It Yourself The app is called Run Card Generator — it’s free on the App Store.
The running analysis prompt (a Claude “Skill” you can install) is open source: github.com/mz462/run-skill
Closing Thought I spent two Saturdays building an iOS app with 98% AI-generated code. It reads from Apple Health, exports workout data, generates art prompts, and supports multiple AI destinations.
It has no AI inside.
And that’s exactly why it was so fast to build, so cheap to run, and so flexible to use.
The smartest AI app might be the one that doesn’t try to be smart at all.

content:
The Problem You have data. Lots of it.
Your team captures everything—sales metrics, customer interactions, product analytics, support tickets. But when someone asks a simple question like “Are we improving?” you’re stuck either:
Clicking through five dashboards and manually connecting dots, or Paying for specialized tools that lock you into their workflows Sound familiar?
I hit this wall with my running data. I was paying $200/year for Strava and Runna (coaching app) but still couldn’t get straight answers to questions like:
“It’s been 2 weeks since NYC Marathon—am I recovering well?” “This same route, how does today compare to last week? Last month?” “How am I performing vs my training plan for Jersey City Half?” The apps gave me charts and pace averages. What I needed was analysis with context.
So I spent a weekend building something different. Not a dashboard. Not another analytics tool. A conversation.
First, I created a Claude Project and loaded it with knowledge:
My personalized training plan (created through earlier Claude discussions) Modern training methodologies (Jack Daniels VDOT, Pfitzinger periodization) My race goals and current phase Then I connected my running database (867 runs worth of history).
Now I can ask: “Analyze my recent run vs my training plan” and get back comprehensive analysis—split-by-split breakdown, heart rate zones, historical comparisons, recovery assessment, personalized recommendations. In seconds.
And now I’m considering canceling both subscriptions.
The technical architecture behind this taught me four concepts that are reshaping how businesses interact with data: MCP, Skills, Subagents, and Prompts.
But more importantly, I learned the unifying principle behind all of them:
Context window is sacred.
Every AI has a limited “working memory” (context window). The breakthrough isn’t making AI smarter—it’s making AI more context-efficient. All four concepts are techniques for managing what gets loaded into that precious context window, and when.
Here’s what they actually mean, and why they matter for your business (explained without the hype).
What I Built (The Context) Before diving into concepts, here’s the setup:
Step 1: Set up project knowledge (using Claude Projects)
Created a dedicated “Running” project in Claude Added my personalized training plan (developed through previous Claude conversations) Included modern training science frameworks (Jack Daniels VDOT, Pfitzinger HR zones, periodization models) This gave the AI baseline context about how to evaluate running performance Step 2: Connected data source (using MCP)
Linked my cloud database containing 867 runs of historical data Enabled the AI to query actual performance metrics, not just theoretical principles Step 3: Built conversational analysis (using Skills + Prompts)
Now I can ask complex questions like “How’s my recovery 2 weeks post-NYC Marathon compared to my training plan?” The AI synthesizes project knowledge + historical data + current metrics into personalized insights What this replaced:
Strava Premium: Basic analytics and social features Runna coaching app: Generic training plans and guidance Combined cost: ~$200/year for services that still felt disconnected from my actual context Next step: I’m exploring building this into an iOS app—turning a weekend proof-of-concept into a product.
The whole project is open source here if you want to see the details.
But the real insight isn’t about running or saving money—it’s about the four architectural building blocks that made this possible in a weekend. These same patterns apply whether you’re analyzing post-marathon recovery, sales pipeline health, or customer support trends.
1. MCP (Model Context Protocol): Why Your Data Silos Are About to Disappear The old way: Copy data from Salesforce, paste into ChatGPT, hope the context is enough.
The new way: AI connects directly to your data sources through standardized “plugs.”
The analogy: Remember when every phone had a different charger? Then USB came along. MCP is USB for AI—a universal standard that lets AI assistants access different data sources seamlessly.
In my project: Instead of uploading CSV files, the AI connects directly to my cloud database (MotherDuck). When I ask “How does today’s run compare to the same route from last week?” it queries 867 runs, filters by route similarity, compares pace/HR trends, and answers contextually. All without me copying/pasting anything.
The power: I can ask “Am I recovering well from NYC Marathon 2 weeks ago?” and it:
Queries my marathon performance (Nov 3, 2024) Pulls my runs from the past 2 weeks Compares heart rate, pace, and distance patterns to typical post-marathon recovery References my training plan to see if I’m on track for Jersey City Half All in one conversational query.
Why this matters for business:
Your Salesforce data + your Google Analytics + your support tickets can all be accessible through one conversational interface. No more:
“Let me pull up that dashboard…” “I’ll export this and send it to you…” “Give me a day to run that report…” The catch: You control permissions. Just like granting app access on your phone, you decide what data the AI can see.
Personal learning: I initially thought I’d need to build custom integrations. MCP meant I just configured a connection string. The infrastructure already exists.
The Claude Project setup was equally important: Without loading my training plan and training science frameworks into project knowledge first, the AI would have no context for how to evaluate my data. It could query numbers, but couldn’t interpret “Is this good recovery?” The combination of project knowledge + MCP data access is what enables real insights.
2. Skills: Capturing Expertise That Usually Lives in Someone’s Head The problem I hit: The AI could access my data, but it didn’t know how runners actually train. It couldn’t tell me if 6:51/km was good for a Zone 2 run.
The solution: I created a “skill”—essentially a playbook that teaches the AI about:
Jack Daniels’ VDOT training methodology Pfitzinger heart rate zones How to evaluate pace progression Training plan periodization (base, build, peak, taper) Now the AI doesn’t just return numbers. It provides coached insights.
The golden rule I learned: If you’re repeating the same instructions across multiple conversations, create a Skill.
Business translation:
Think about the expertise that exists only in your top performer’s head:
Your best salesperson’s qualification methodology Your financial analyst’s forecasting approach Your customer success team’s escalation protocol What if that expertise became a reusable skill that everyone could access through conversation?
Real examples:
Brand standards skill: Upload guidelines once. Every document, email, and presentation automatically follows your color palette, typography, tone. Compliance skill: Ensure every customer data request follows GDPR protocols without training every employee on the full legal framework. Excel analysis skill: Your senior analyst’s pivot table methodology becomes accessible to the whole team. The efficiency trick: Skills use “progressive disclosure”—a quick preview loads first (like a table of contents), full instructions load only when needed. You can maintain dozens of specialized skills without slowing anything down.
The context efficiency breakthrough: Skills can also contain actual code and scripts. Instead of the AI rewriting the same data processing code every time, the skill stores it. The AI just needs to know:
When to use the tool How to call it How to interpret results Example from my project: My VDOT calculation formula lives in the skill. The AI doesn’t regenerate the formula each time—it just calls the function and interprets the output. Saves hundreds of tokens per query.
Important clarification: Skills aren’t exclusive to Claude. The concept of reusable skills is universal. You could take my running analysis skill and use it with ChatGPT, Gemini, or any other AI—just paste the instructions and code into the context window.
The difference is architectural:
Claude engineered Skills to be context-efficient: They’re loaded into a “container” that sits outside your main context window. Only the relevant skill loads when needed. Other platforms require everything in context: You’d paste your skill instructions at the start of every conversation. It works, but consumes context window space the entire time, even when not actively being used. The trade-off: Claude’s approach optimizes context (you can have dozens of skills without slowdown), but locks you into their platform. Pasting into ChatGPT is platform-agnostic, but less efficient.
Why this matters for builders: When architecting AI systems, think about whether your “skills” need to be platform-specific or portable. Sometimes you optimize for performance (Claude Skills), sometimes for portability (copy-paste instructions).
The ROI moment: When my system started giving me better insights than the $200/year in apps I was paying for, I realized this wasn’t just a technical exercise—it was a business model shift. Why pay for generic SaaS when you can build personalized AI on your own data?
3. Subagents: The Plumber You Hire for Results, Not Process The concept: When your sink is clogged, you don’t micromanage the plumber (“use the snake now, try the auger next”). You want to know: “Is it fixed? What caused it? How do I prevent this?”
The plumber handles the details. You get the outcome.
How this works with AI:
Imagine asking: “Create a comprehensive competitive analysis.”
Instead of one AI trying to do everything sequentially, it simultaneously delegates to specialists:
Market research subagent → Gathers competitor data (done in 8 seconds) Financial analysis subagent → Models revenue trends (done in 6 seconds) SWOT subagent → Identifies strengths/weaknesses (done in 5 seconds) Each reports back with findings + recommendations. The main AI synthesizes into one report. Total time: 8 seconds (not 19 seconds sequential).
My running project doesn’t use this yet (currently one analyzer does everything sequentially), but it could. If I asked for a comprehensive training review, subagents could handle:
Historical performance trends (Database Explorer) Pace consistency analysis (Pace Analyzer) Fitness trajectory modeling (VO2 Max Calculator) Heart rate zone evaluation (Training Science) All in parallel, each reporting back just the insights.
Why business leaders should care:
Speed through parallelization: Complex analysis that took hours now takes seconds Context window efficiency: Each subagent operates in its own context, preventing the main conversation from getting cluttered with irrelevant details Stay focused on outcomes: You don’t wade through every calculation—you just get synthesized insights Automatic expertise matching: Refund questions → billing specialist, technical issues → product specialist Scalability: Same infrastructure handles one request or a thousand The context insight: Without subagents, one AI tries to hold everything in its working memory—database queries, pace calculations, heart rate analysis, training plan context. With subagents, each specialist handles their domain and reports back just the insights. Much more efficient.
Confirmed capability: I researched this—both Claude Code and the Agent SDK support parallel subagents (limit ~10 concurrent). This isn’t theoretical, it’s production-ready.
4. Prompts: The Difference Between “Run a Report” and “Give Me Insights” The realization: Prompts aren’t just questions anymore. They’re job descriptions.
Compare these two:
Basic: “Analyze my run”
Detailed: “Analyze my November 16th run. Provide: (1) split-by-split breakdown with pace progression, (2) heart rate zone analysis with drift calculation, (3) comparison to similar historical runs in the ±20% distance range, (4) evaluation against my current training plan phase, (5) specific recommendations for next workouts.”
The second isn’t just “more detailed”—it’s a reusable template that ensures consistent, comprehensive analysis every time.
The business parallel:
Think about recurring tasks your team does:
Quarterly business reviews Customer onboarding workflows Code review checklists Sales qualification Each has an implicit structure in someone’s head. Prompts make that structure explicit and repeatable.
What I learned building this:
Good prompts are the new SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures). They:
Ensure consistency at scale Capture quality standards Let junior employees produce senior-level work Prevent “garbage in, garbage out” The pattern: Start vague, refine through iteration, capture the refined version as a template.
A workflow feature I can’t live without: Prompt editing Here’s where Claude’s UX shines. When you get a mediocre response, you can go back to any previous prompt in the conversation, edit it, and regenerate from that point forward.
Why this matters: The earlier you steer the conversation in the right direction, the better your results. If I realize at message #10 that my prompt at message #3 was unclear, I can go back and fix it without starting over.
The version control advantage: Claude keeps all previous versions so you can compare improvements. Did my edit make the response better or worse? I can check.
Example from my running analysis:
Original prompt: “Analyze my run” Got generic stats Edited prompt #3 to: “Analyze my run. Compare pace to similar post-marathon recovery runs, evaluate heart rate zones against base-building targets, and assess weekly volume vs training plan.” Much better response Could compare both versions to see the difference Why I haven’t fully adopted other platforms:
Google Gemini only lets you edit the most recent prompt ChatGPT doesn’t show previous versions for comparison This workflow optimization has slowed my adoption of competitors The meta-insight: Good tools don’t just execute prompts—they help you iterate on them efficiently. This is the difference between using AI and getting good at using AI.
Putting It Together: When to Use What Still confused about which tool does what? Here’s the framework I use:
The unifying theme: All four techniques optimize what goes into the AI’s limited “working memory” and when.
In my running project:
MCP: ✅ Connects to my cloud database (only queries relevant runs) Skill: ✅ Stores training science code + methodology (AI doesn’t regenerate formulas) Prompts: ✅ Structured analysis requests (gets exactly what I need, no fluff) Subagents: ⏳ Not implemented yet, but would isolate specialized analysis in separate contexts Even with three of four, the system transformed how I interact with my data.
The Before/After That Made This Real Before:
$200/year for Strava + Runna subscriptions Generic training plans that didn’t adapt to my actual performance 867 runs of data sitting in files with no meaningful synthesis Questions like “How’s my marathon recovery?” required exporting data to CSV, pivot tables, chart creation Advice disconnected from my specific context (2 weeks post-NYC Marathon, training for Jersey City Half, sub-1:30:00 goal) After:
Ask questions in plain English: “How’s my recovery 2 weeks post-NYC Marathon?” Get personalized, science-backed insights in seconds: heart rate trends, pace comparisons vs pre-marathon baseline, weekly volume progression Coaching that understands my 867-run history AND my current training phase (recovery → base building) “Was this a good run?” gets answered with multi-dimensional context: 23% faster than similar post-marathon runs, Zone 2 heart rate (perfect for recovery phase), weekly volume at 11.9km vs plan target of 40km Close to canceling both subscriptions (saving $200/year) The kicker: I’m now exploring building this into an iOS app for other runners. A weekend proof-of-concept might become a product.
The business equivalent:
Replace “running data” with “sales pipeline,” “customer support tickets,” or “supply chain metrics.”
Same transformation: From data overwhelm + expensive point solutions → conversational insights built on your data.
The Bigger Picture: What This Means for How We Work We’re moving from:
Clicking through dashboards → Asking questions Hiring specialists for every analysis → Deploying reusable skills Copying data between tools → Connecting via MCP Waiting for sequential analysis → Delegating to parallel subagents But the deeper shift is this: We’re learning to treat context window like RAM.
Just like computer programmers optimize memory usage, we now need to think about:
What knowledge should be loaded upfront (Project knowledge, Skills)? What data should be fetched on-demand (MCP)? What tasks should run in isolated contexts (Subagents)? How do we structure requests to get exactly what we need (Prompts)? The question isn’t whether AI will change your industry. It’s whether you’ll understand the building blocks well enough to shape that change.
Three Questions to Ask Your Team Monday Morning What data do we have that’s underutilized because it’s hard to access?
(That’s your MCP opportunity)
What expertise exists in someone’s head that should be captured as a reusable skill?
(That’s your Skills opportunity)
What repetitive analysis could we turn into a conversational question?
(That’s your Prompts opportunity)
The tools are here. The infrastructure is ready.
Want to See How This Actually Works? The entire project is open source: github.com/mz462/run-skill
Even if you’re not a runner or a coder:
See how Skills are structured (the methodology applies to any domain) Explore how MCP connects AI to databases Understand how prompts evolve from simple questions to powerful instructions P.S. - If you’re exploring AI in your organization and want to discuss practical applications (not hype), let’s connect. I’m particularly interested in how teams are thinking about agent platforms and orchestration—and how vertical AI apps might disrupt existing SaaS markets.

On October 16, 2025, while the tech world was still digesting OpenAI’s Instant Checkout within ChatGPT, Anthropic quietly released something called “Skills.”
No flashy demos. No performance charts comparing against GPT-5. Just a simple announcement about folders containing Markdown files and optional scripts.
Within hours, Simon Willison—one of the most productive voices in AI development—called it “maybe a bigger deal than MCP.”
Here’s what makes this strange: Claude has only 5% of ChatGPT’s user base. But it generates 40% of OpenAI’s revenue.
How does a company that launched 3.5 months after ChatGPT, with a fraction of the users, keep forcing the industry leader to follow its playbook? How does the underdog with 18.9 million monthly users compete against a giant with 800 million weekly users—and somehow capture nearly half the revenue?
The answer isn’t about who has the best model. It’s not about who ships features fastest, or who raises more funding, or who has the most compute.
It’s about something far more interesting: seeing combinations that everyone else missed.
The Relentless Treadmill June 2024: Anthropic releases Artifacts—a split-screen interface that lets you edit code and documents while chatting with Claude.
October 2024: OpenAI ships Canvas. Four months later. Same concept.
September 2024: OpenAI launches o1, its first reasoning model that “thinks” before answering.
February 2025: Claude releases Extended Thinking. Five months later. Same capability.
February 2025: OpenAI introduces Deep Research—an agent that scours the web for comprehensive reports.
April 2025: Claude ships its Research feature. Two months later.
This is what the AI arms race looks like in 2024-2025. A feature released today becomes table stakes in 2-5 months.
The pattern is relentless. It’s exhausting just to watch. Here’s the full timeline of how these two companies have traded punches:
Date Company Product/Feature What It Does Nov 30, 2022 OpenAI ChatGPT Launch Conversational AI; reached 1M users in 5 days Mar 14, 2023 OpenAI GPT-4 Multimodal model with enhanced reasoning Mar 14, 2023 Anthropic Claude 1 First Claude release; 9K context window Jul 11, 2023 Anthropic Claude 2 100K token context window; public availability Jul 6, 2023 OpenAI Code Interpreter Data analysis, code execution in containers Aug 28, 2023 OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise Unlimited GPT-4, 32K context, enterprise features Sep 7, 2023 Anthropic Claude Pro $20/month subscription matching ChatGPT Plus Nov 21, 2023 Anthropic Claude 2.1 200K context window (2x GPT-4 Turbo) Mar 4, 2024 Anthropic Claude 3 Family Three-tier models; 200K context; new benchmarks May 13, 2024 OpenAI GPT-4o “Omni” multimodal; 2x faster, 50% cheaper Jun 20, 2024 Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet + Artifacts Split-screen collaborative editing Sep 4, 2024 Anthropic Claude Enterprise 500K context window; GitHub integration Sep 12, 2024 OpenAI o1-preview + o1-mini Reasoning models with “thinking” capability Oct 3, 2024 OpenAI Canvas Writing/coding collaboration interface Oct 22, 2024 Anthropic Computer Use Control computers via screen/keyboard/mouse Dec 5, 2024 OpenAI ChatGPT Pro + o1 Full $200/month plan; o1 out of preview Feb 2, 2025 OpenAI Deep Research Autonomous research with web crawling Feb 24, 2025 Anthropic Claude 3.7 + Extended Thinking Reasoning with visible step-by-step process Apr 15, 2025 Anthropic Claude Research Multi-step research across internal/external sources Sep 29, 2025 Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5 + Code 2.0 Enhanced model; major CLI update Oct 16, 2025 Anthropic Skills Customizable folders with instructions & scripts Look at that table. The conventional wisdom is obvious: This is a speed contest. Whoever ships features fastest wins. The treadmill never stops. Innovation means being first.
And on the surface, the numbers seem to confirm OpenAI’s dominance. ChatGPT has 800 million weekly users. Claude has 18.9 million monthly users—roughly 5% of ChatGPT’s scale.
OpenAI raised billions. They have the compute. They have the users. They have the brand recognition.
By every conventional metric, Anthropic is the underdog playing catch-up.
But zoom out, and a different story emerges.
Yes, both companies are matching each other’s features with brutal efficiency. But look closer at how Anthropic innovates, and you’ll notice something peculiar.
They’re not trying to outrun OpenAI.
They’re trying to out-see them.
The Evolution That Reveals Everything To understand what Anthropic is really doing, you need to look at how they approached one specific problem: code execution.
October 2024. Claude launched its first code execution feature, called the “analysis tool.”
It wasn’t Python in containers like OpenAI’s Code Interpreter. It was JavaScript. Running in your browser.
The code executed in a locked-down Web Worker that could only communicate back to the main page by intercepting messages sent to console.log(). It could read files you uploaded using fs.readFile(). It had access to Lodash and Papa Parse for working with data.
That’s it.
Simon Willison, who has documented every major AI development since GPT-3, wrote detailed technical notes about it. The implementation was clever—secure, fast, no server costs. But compared to OpenAI’s full Python environment with data analysis libraries?
It seemed… modest.
September 2025. Claude pivoted entirely.
Now it had server-side containers just like OpenAI: Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.12, Node.js, 9GB of RAM, 5GB of disk space. The full setup. It could install packages from npm and PyPI. It could run shell commands.
The browser JavaScript approach was gone. This was the real deal.
This looked like catching up. Like Anthropic finally admitted OpenAI’s architecture was right and copied it.
October 16, 2025. Skills launched.
And suddenly, the pattern became clear.
Skills aren’t just about running code in containers. They’re about systematically initializing those containers with the files and tools users actually need.
Pre-installed LibreOffice for manipulating PowerPoint, Word, and Excel files. Automatic file management for office documents. Skills that can apply company branding to presentations. Skills that review contracts against legal policies. Skills that format Excel formulas to match corporate standards.
Not just data analysis. Actual work.
Here’s the insight that changes everything:
OpenAI pioneered LLMs plus containers back in July 2023 with Code Interpreter. Andrej Karpathy called it “your personal data analyst.” Everyone saw the obvious use case: upload a CSV, generate charts, analyze data, create visualizations.
Impressive. Worthy of a keynote demo.
But Anthropic’s product team asked a different question:
Where does work actually happen?
Not in Jupyter notebooks analyzing datasets. Not in creating one-off data visualizations.
In PowerPoint decks for client presentations. In Word documents with tracked changes and legal reviews. In Excel spreadsheets with company-specific formulas and formatting standards.
The technology—containers plus LLMs—already existed. The genius was seeing what to put inside.
This is the turning point. The moment where copying becomes innovating. Where “catching up” becomes “leapfrogging.”
Because OpenAI solved for data scientists doing impressive things.
Anthropic solved for everyone who’s ever had to format a PowerPoint at 11 PM before a client meeting.
How They Did It So how does a company with a fraction of the users compete against a giant? Not by trying to beat them at their own game. By playing a different game entirely.
Start Where It’s Easy, Learn What Matters The browser JavaScript approach wasn’t a compromise. It was a probe.
Think about what Anthropic learned in October 2024: They shipped code execution in weeks, not months. No infrastructure complexity. No security nightmares from running arbitrary code on their servers. Just watch what users actually do with code execution and learn the patterns.
This is classic product strategy: Start with the simplest thing that could possibly work.
While OpenAI had already spent over a year running Python containers at scale, Anthropic was learning something more valuable: What do users actually need code execution for?
Turns out, most people weren’t running complex data science pipelines. They were doing simpler tasks. Parsing data. Formatting outputs. Generating structured content.
The browser approach taught Anthropic what mattered. And what could wait.
Match the Table Stakes, Build the Foundation By September 2025, containers became non-negotiable. Every serious AI assistant needed server-side code execution. The market had spoken.
So Anthropic built it. Ubuntu containers. Python and Node.js. Package installation. The works.
But here’s what separates good product teams from great ones: While building container infrastructure, Anthropic wasn’t asking “how do we match Code Interpreter?”
They were asking: “Now that we have containers, what becomes possible?”
This is the difference between playing catch-up and playing chess. You match the table stakes not because you’re copying, but because you’re building the foundation for your next move.
The container infrastructure wasn’t the destination. It was the platform.
Find the Adjacent Possible This is where Skills gets brilliant.
The architecture is almost offensively simple. A Markdown file with YAML frontmatter. Optional scripts. Optional supporting documents. That’s it.
No complex protocol specifications like MCP (Model Context Protocol), which requires hosts, clients, servers, and multiple transport layers. No tens of thousands of tokens of protocol overhead. Just Markdown files that Claude can read and understand.
But here’s what makes it powerful:
Progressive disclosure. When you start a conversation with Claude, it scans available skills and reads just the names and brief descriptions—consuming only dozens of tokens per skill. Only when a skill becomes relevant does Claude load the full details. Compare this to MCP implementations that can consume tens of thousands of context tokens just for the protocol overhead, leaving limited space for actual work.
Portable by design. The same skill format works across Claude.ai, Claude Code CLI, and the API. No special infrastructure needed. If you can write a Markdown file, you can create a skill. Simon Willison predicts “a Cambrian explosion in Skills” precisely because the barrier to entry is so low.
Composable. Multiple skills load automatically when relevant. Claude coordinates them without you having to specify which ones to use. It’s intelligent orchestration, not manual configuration.
Language-agnostic. Skills can include code in any language the container environment supports. Python for data processing. JavaScript for web interactions. Bash scripts for system operations. Whatever solves the problem.
This is what “finding the adjacent possible” looks like in practice. The technology—containers, Markdown, YAML—all existed. The innovation was seeing how to combine them.
Solve for Where the Work Lives And here’s the masterstroke: Pre-installing LibreOffice in the container environment.
It sounds almost boring, doesn’t it? LibreOffice? The open-source office suite?
But think about what this unlocks:
A skill that formats Excel formulas correctly and applies corporate financial models A skill that creates PowerPoint presentations from scratch or templates, with proper branding A skill that edits Word documents with tracked changes, following legal review processes A skill that fills PDF forms and extracts structured data These aren’t edge cases. This is where work lives.
OpenAI’s Code Interpreter solved for data scientists creating impressive visualizations. Important work. But niche.
Skills solve for everyone who’s ever needed to:
Generate a client proposal in the company’s PowerPoint template Review a contract and flag clauses that violate company policy Create a financial model in Excel with the right formulas and formatting Produce a report with tracked changes for legal review When Anthropic added LibreOffice to containers, they weren’t adding features. They were unlocking workflows.
Because containers plus LLMs had existed for over two years. Everyone could have pre-installed LibreOffice. No one did.
Why?
Because everyone was solving for the impressive demo, not the daily workflow.
Data analysis and chart generation make for great keynote presentations. Properly formatting PowerPoint slides with your company’s brand guidelines? Boring. Unsexy.
But that’s where the revenue is. That’s where businesses will pay. That’s where Claude’s 40% revenue share with 5% of the users comes from.
Anthropic didn’t invent new technology. They saw combinations others missed.
The Numbers That Tell the Real Story Let’s return to that opening paradox: Claude has 18.9 million monthly active users. ChatGPT has 800 million weekly active users.
Claude is 5% of ChatGPT’s scale.
Yet Anthropic hit $4 billion in annualized revenue by mid-2025—40% of OpenAI’s revenue.
How?
Because the users Claude wins are the ones doing work, not exploration.
The data backs this up. Look at what people actually use each AI for:
36% of Claude conversations involve computer programming and software development 4.2% of ChatGPT conversations are coding-related ChatGPT is a consumer product. It’s for creative writing, general questions, homework help, casual exploration. Eight hundred million people asking “write me a poem about my cat.”
Claude is a productivity tool. It’s for developers writing code. Product managers drafting specifications. Lawyers reviewing contracts. Consultants building client presentations at midnight.
This is the real competitive moat. Not who has more users, but who owns the workflows that businesses will pay for.
The Pattern Recognition Insight Look back at what Anthropic has pioneered over the past 18 months:
Artifacts (June 2024): A split-screen interface for iterative editing. Became a must-have so fast that OpenAI shipped Canvas four months later.
Computer Use (October 2024): The first frontier model that can control computers via screen, keyboard, and mouse interactions. Still industry-leading.
Skills (October 2025): Simon Willison predicts “a Cambrian explosion” in adoption, potentially exceeding MCP precisely because it’s so simple.
These aren’t random features. They share a philosophy:
The best product teams don’t invent new technology. They see combinations others missed.
Containers plus LLMs had existed for over two years. Anyone could have pre-installed LibreOffice. The technology was sitting there, waiting.
But everyone was optimizing for the wrong thing.
OpenAI optimized for the impressive demo—data analysis, chart generation, “your personal data analyst.” Perfect for a keynote. Perfect for going viral on Twitter.
Anthropic optimized for the daily workflow—PowerPoint with company branding, Word documents with legal review, Excel with corporate formulas. Boring. Unsexy.
But that’s where the money is.
Two Diverging Paths Here’s what’s becoming clear as we enter late 2025: These companies are no longer competing for the same game.
OpenAI is doubling down on consumer scale. The recent App SDK lets developers build custom applications on top of ChatGPT. The Memory feature learns your preferences across conversations. They’re building a platform for 800 million users to do… more things. More broadly. More consumer-facing.
It’s the toC (to-Consumer) playbook: Maximize reach, viral features, everyday use cases. Be the AI everyone has heard of.
Anthropic is sharpening its focus on business workflows. Skills aren’t designed for casual users—they’re for companies that need Claude to follow specific procedures. Computer Use isn’t for browsing memes—it’s for automating business processes. Extended Thinking with visible reasoning isn’t for fun—it’s for enterprise customers who need to audit AI decisions.
It’s the toB (to-Business) playbook: Maximize value per user, workflow integration, enterprise requirements. Be the AI that companies can’t live without.
This explains the revenue paradox perfectly. OpenAI has the users. Anthropic has the paying users.
ChatGPT is building to be ubiquitous. Claude is building to be indispensable.
What This Means for the AI Race The lesson from Anthropic’s trajectory isn’t about playing catch-up or moving faster. It’s about pattern recognition as competitive strategy.
In early 2023, when Claude launched 3.5 months after ChatGPT’s viral explosion, the obvious path was: Copy what works. Match features. Compete on speed.
Instead, Anthropic asked different questions:
Not “how do we make data analysis impressive?” but “where does work actually happen?” Not “how do we get more users?” but “which users will pay for this?” Not “how do we beat OpenAI’s features?” but “what combinations are they missing?” This is product strategy at its finest. Seeing what already exists. Recognizing patterns others overlook. Combining pieces in ways that unlock new value.
The technology for Skills—containers, Markdown files, YAML, LibreOffice—was all there. The insight was asking: What if we systematically initialized containers with business tools instead of just data science libraries?
One question. One combination. A $4 billion revenue run rate.
The Bigger Game The AI race isn’t about who builds the biggest model. It’s not about who ships features fastest. It’s not even about who has the most users.
It’s about who sees where the work actually lives—and builds for that.
For two years, everyone with containers and LLMs solved for data scientists making charts. Important work. But narrow.
Anthropic looked at the same technology and saw PowerPoint presentations. Word documents. Excel spreadsheets. The unglamorous, everyday work that businesses actually pay for.
They saw the combination everyone else missed.
And now, with only 5% of the users, they’re capturing 40% of the revenue.
The next wave of AI won’t be won by who has the most compute or the largest context window.
It will be won by who recognizes patterns others can’t see. Who finds combinations that unlock work others aren’t even looking at.
Anthropic isn’t trying to outrun OpenAI in a features race.
They’re playing a different game entirely.
And judging by the numbers?
They’re winning.

The Nature Editorial That Caught My Eye A recent Nature Reviews Bioengineering editorial titled “Writing is Thinking” made a compelling case for preserving human-written scientific papers in the age of large language models. The editorial argues that writing isn’t merely about reporting results—it’s a cognitive tool that helps us uncover new thoughts and ideas.
As the editorial puts it: “Writing compels us to think—not in the chaotic, non-linear way our minds typically wander, but in a structured, intentional manner.” This resonated deeply with me, especially as someone who started this blog as a way to maintain “conscious effort” in my thinking.
What struck me most was the editorial’s suggestion that if writing is thinking, then when we read AI-generated text, are we reading the “thoughts” of an LLM rather than the researchers behind the paper? This question sent me down a rabbit hole, exploring the fundamental differences between human writing and AI text generation.
Expanding Beyond Context Windows: The Human Drive As I reflected on the editorial, I realized something important about why humans write: we’re fundamentally driven to expand beyond our context windows.
When I write, I’m not simply organizing what I already know—I’m actively seeking to transcend my limitations. I write to discover connections I hadn’t previously made, to extend my understanding beyond what’s immediately visible to me. The very struggle of articulating thoughts forces me to reach beyond my current knowledge boundaries.
This is perhaps our defining characteristic as humans. We climb mountains “because they’re there,” we explore space, we create art that challenges perception, and we develop theories about realms we can’t directly observe. This constant pushing against the boundaries of what we know drives human creativity and progress.
The physical act of writing—whether typing on a keyboard or scribbling in a notebook—becomes the vehicle through which we expand our context window. It’s a tool for transcending our cognitive limitations.
Optimizing Within Constraints: The AI Approach LLMs, in contrast, are designed fundamentally differently. They operate by optimizing within constraints rather than trying to transcend them.
In my previous post “Why Can’t LLMs Say ‘I Don’t Know’?”, I explored how current AI models struggle with recognizing their knowledge boundaries. They lack the intrinsic drive to question or expand their boundaries—they simply make the best statistical predictions possible within the parameters they’ve been given.
The Nature editorial mentions this phenomenon as “hallucination”—when LLMs generate incorrect information confidently. This happens precisely because they lack what I think of as a proper “loss function” for being wrong. They face no real consequences for errors beyond what’s encoded in their training.
This fundamental difference shapes everything about how LLMs generate text versus how humans write. LLMs don’t write to discover—they write to predict the most statistically likely next word based on their training data and immediate context.
The Missing Element: Intuition and Embodied Knowledge There’s always something subtly missing in AI-generated text that’s difficult to articulate. Despite technical proficiency, LLM writing often lacks what we might call soul or intuition.
Intuition—knowledge without conscious reasoning—emerges from our embodied experiences, unconscious pattern recognition, and evolutionary adaptations. It manifests as gut feelings, sudden insights, or inexplicable certainties that later prove valuable.
What makes human intuition so powerful is that it integrates multiple forms of knowledge:
Explicit knowledge we can articulate Tacit knowledge we’ve absorbed but can’t fully explain Embodied knowledge stored in our physical responses Social knowledge about human dynamics LLMs fundamentally lack physical presence. They can only “understand” concepts like gravity or exhilaration through textual descriptions rather than lived sensory experience. They have no skin in the game—no physical consequences for being wrong that might drive caution or accuracy.
When humans write, our thoughts are grounded in physical experience and constrained by social consequences. Our writing carries traces of this embodied intuition that algorithms simply can’t replicate.
The Social Dimension of Writing I’ve often noticed the peculiar tension we feel when others read our writing—a simultaneous desire for our thoughts to be found and fear of judgment. This productive embarrassment creates a unique cognitive pressure that machines don’t experience.
The anticipation of human readers drives us to refine our ideas more carefully than we might when thinking privately. We question our assumptions, strengthen our arguments, and clarify our reasoning precisely because we know others will scrutinize them.
LLMs lack this emotional stake in their outputs. They don’t feel vulnerable when generating text, so they miss this crucial dimension of human writing—the emotional pressure that forces clarity and intellectual honesty.
Current instruction-tuned models are fundamentally designed to agree and be helpful rather than to push back or challenge users’ assumptions. They prioritize agreement over intellectual integrity, which creates an asymmetric relationship fundamentally different from productive human writing partnerships, where editors and colleagues challenge our ideas through productive disagreement.
Finding Balance: Human Agency in AI-Assisted Writing Using LLMs effectively requires constant awareness that I’m driving the conversation, not the AI. It’s dangerous to mistake LLMs for intelligent beings with genuine understanding or metacognition.
The editorial acknowledges that LLMs can serve as valuable tools in scientific writing—improving readability, assisting with grammar, searching and summarizing literature, providing bullet points for brainstorming, and helping overcome writer’s block.
I’ve found this to be true in my own writing process. AI tools can generate ideas, help structure thoughts, and assist with editing. But the crucial element is maintaining human agency throughout the process—using LLMs as generative tools while maintaining rigorous human verification.
This approach preserves the cognitive benefits outlined in the Nature editorial while leveraging AI capabilities. The writing process itself should remain human-driven to maintain its power as a thinking tool.
Writing as Metacognition The Nature editorial concludes with a powerful statement: “Outsourcing the entire writing process to LLMs may deprive us of the opportunity to reflect on our field and engage in the creative, essential task of shaping research findings into a compelling narrative—a skill that is certainly important beyond scholarly writing and publishing.”
I believe this insight extends far beyond academic writing. Writing is one of our most powerful tools for metacognition—thinking about our own thinking. When I write, I become aware of the boundaries of my knowledge in ways that simply thinking about a topic doesn’t accomplish.
This metacognitive awareness is precisely what LLMs lack. They can’t step back and assess their own knowledge state or recognize when they’re reaching beyond their capabilities. They’re pattern-matching machines without self-awareness.
Context Engineers of Our Own Understanding Perhaps the most profound difference I’ve realized through this exploration is this: humans write to expand their context window, while machines write to optimize within it.
When I sit down to write about a complex topic like this one, I’m not just organizing my existing thoughts—I’m actively expanding my understanding, making new connections, and discovering insights I didn’t have when I started typing. The struggle is productive precisely because it pushes me beyond what I already know.
As we navigate this new era of AI-assisted writing, maintaining this distinction is crucial. We must remain the context engineers of our own understanding—using AI as a tool while preserving the uniquely human cognitive benefits that come from the conscious effort of writing.
After all, if writing is thinking, I’d rather do my own thinking, thank you very much.

When Dad Becomes Your Research Assistant My dad texted me a photo yesterday from his antique shop. “Found this old Cantonese children’s book from the 1920s,” he said. “Thought you might find it interesting.”
I opened the image and immediately felt that familiar mix of nostalgia and confusion. I could mostly read it—traditional Chinese characters arranged in neat columns, reading right to left, top to bottom. But there were nuances I wasn’t catching, cultural references that felt just out of reach.
The page that started it all: A 1920s Cantonese children’s book that reads “西瓜共蟹，吾識莫買；咸魚臘肉，見火就熟” (Watermelons and crabs, if you don’t know, don’t buy; salted fish and cured meat, cook when they see fire). The text teaches practical market wisdom—advising beginners to avoid complex purchases like watermelons and crabs that require knowledge to choose well, and instead start with simple ingredients like salted fish and cured meat that are easy to prepare. What made it even more intriguing was the lesson number written in 苏州码 (Suzhou numerals)—a traditional Chinese commercial notation system dating back to the Southern Song period that I had to research to understand1. It’s a charming slice of 1920s street-smart learning with layers of cultural complexity.
Perfect job for AI, right?
Plot Twist: I Became My Own Research Assistant While waiting for Claude to process the image, I got impatient. A quick Google search about 1920s Cantonese children’s literature led me down a fascinating rabbit hole. Within 20 minutes, I had fully decoded the text, understood the cultural context, and even learned about the Republican era’s literacy campaigns.
Then Claude came back with its response.
“I can see this appears to be Chinese text, but I’m having difficulty making out the specific characters…”
Wait. What?
The Great AI Stress Test That’s when things got interesting. If one AI couldn’t handle this, what about the others? I decided to run my own little experiment:
OpenAI O3: Nailed it. Not only read every character correctly but explained the cultural context and even noted the historical significance of the reading direction.
Google Gemini 2.5 Pro: Partial credit. Could recognize most characters but completely missed the meaning and cultural nuances.
Claude Opus: Epic fail. Couldn’t even identify half the characters, let alone understand what it was looking at.
Here’s the kicker: any modern Cantonese speaker can read this 100-year-old text without breaking a sweat. But two of our most advanced AI systems? Total confusion.
The Linguistic Time Machine This little discovery sent me down another research spiral. Turns out, this isn’t just a random old book—it’s a testament to the remarkable stability of written Chinese over the past century.
The traditional Chinese character system has remained essentially unchanged since the Han dynasty around 200 BCE2. By the 1920s, when this book was published, written Cantonese had developed into a well-recognized system, particularly with the rise of Cantonese opera libretti3. The Republican era was also a time of significant literacy campaigns and children’s book publishing, making materials like this crucial for understanding both language preservation and cultural transmission4.
What’s fascinating is that modern Cantonese speakers in Hong Kong, Macau, and overseas communities can effortlessly read these century-old texts, thanks to the continued use of traditional characters and the stability of the writing system5. It’s like having a linguistic time machine that works perfectly for humans but apparently breaks AI.
The Lightbulb Moment Staring at these results, I realized something wild: I might have accidentally discovered the perfect AI benchmark.
Think about it:
Layout Challenge: Can AI understand traditional reading patterns (right-to-left, top-to-bottom)? Character Recognition: Can it handle traditional Chinese in historical context? Cultural Comprehension: Can it grasp the deeper meaning and cultural references? This tiny children’s book had just exposed massive blind spots in billion-dollar AI systems.
Recent research shows that Cantonese remains significantly under-resourced in AI development despite being spoken by over 85 million people worldwide6. The challenges are compounded when dealing with historical texts, where OCR systems struggle with variations in handwriting, printing styles, complex layouts, and the sheer number of character types needed for useful recognition7.
The Wild Idea That Won’t Leave Me Alone What started as “let me ask AI for help” became “wait… did I just accidentally discover something?”
Staring at these results, this crazy thought hit me: What if this little book is the perfect AI stress test?
Think about it:
Any Cantonese speaker can read this effortlessly Two of the world’s best AIs completely failed I’m sitting in a shop that… wait, how many of these do we actually have? I keep thinking… wouldn’t it be fun to build CantoBench? A benchmark where 1920s children’s homework stumps billion-dollar AI models:
Level 1: Can you read right-to-left, top-to-bottom? Level 2: Can you transcribe these historical characters?
Level 3: Can you understand what great-grandma was actually trying to teach?
I mean, I should probably dig through the shop first and see what we’ve got. Maybe this was just a lucky find, or maybe we’re sitting on a goldmine of AI-breaking historical materials.
Either way, the idea is kind of delicious, right?
What This Reveals About AI’s Blind Spots The performance differences between O3, Gemini, and Claude on this simple text reveal something important about current AI limitations. O3’s success likely stems from its advanced reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning and what OpenAI calls “thinking with images”—the ability to integrate visual information directly into its reasoning process rather than just converting images to text8.
Meanwhile, research shows that even advanced models like Gemini 2.5 Pro can struggle with language switching and context preservation in multilingual scenarios9. The challenges are even greater for under-resourced languages and historical texts, where training data is scarce and cultural context is crucial.
This isn’t just about technical capabilities—it’s about cultural preservation. As AI becomes increasingly important for digitizing and preserving historical documents, these blind spots could mean that millions of cultural artifacts remain inaccessible to future digital preservation efforts10.
When Your Dad Accidentally Becomes an AI Researcher For now, I’m just enjoying this weird moment where my dad’s random antique shop photo exposed something fascinating about our most advanced AI systems.
Maybe I’ll put some effort into this—either convince my dad to dig through more materials in China, or find some way to explore what other AI kryptonite might be hiding in that shop. Who knows what we might discover?
Sometimes the best discoveries happen when you’re just trying to understand your great-grandfather’s homework. And sometimes, the most important questions come from the most unexpected places—like a dusty corner of an antique shop where the past meets the future in ways we never imagined.
Who knew a 100-year-old children’s book could be such an AI troublemaker?
