I just read an excellent deep dive from the Manus team about context engineering for AI agents, and it’s packed with practical insights that anyone building AI systems should know about.
The Core Insight The Manus post1 opens with a striking observation: “Most agent failures are not model failures anymore, they are context failures.” We’ve moved past the era where model limitations were the primary bottleneck. Today’s models are remarkably capable—the challenge is giving them the right information at the right time.
They define context engineering as “the discipline of designing and building dynamic systems that provides the right information and tools, in the right format, at the right time, to give a LLM everything it needs to accomplish a task.” Notice that word: dynamic. This isn’t about crafting perfect static prompts—it’s about building systems that evolve context throughout an interaction.
The Hidden Meta-Insight: Agents Are REP Loops, Not Brains After digesting the Manus post more deeply, I realized there’s a fundamental meta-insight that runs throughout their approach but is never explicitly stated: Agents are REP Loops, not brains.
This isn’t a minor technical detail—it’s a complete paradigm shift in how we should think about AI agents. We need to stop thinking of them as autonomous entities with free will and start thinking of them as incredibly powerful REPL systems (Read-Eval-Print Loops):
Read: The carefully constructed context you provide Eval: Based on that context, the agent decides its next action Print: It outputs the action and results back into the context, starting the next loop You’re not teaching a student—you’re writing an input script for a supercomputer. All your work should revolve around making each step of this loop clear, predictable, and debuggable.
The Ultimate Framework: Context Engineering = Memory + Environment + Feedback The Manus approach reveals a systematic framework built around three pillars:
Memory: How to efficiently store and retrieve successful and failed experiences, working in harmony with KV-Cache Environment: Providing the agent with an interactive, persistent workspace (like a file system) Feedback: Injecting the results of actions (whether successful or failed) as input for the next decision cycle Production Lessons Learned the Hard Way 1. Design for KV-Cache Above All Else In production AI agents, there’s one metric that matters more than anything: KV-Cache hit rate. Every step your agent takes grows the context massively, while outputs (usually tool calls) stay short. At Manus, this input-to-output token ratio is 100:1. Every cache miss means 10x cost explosion.
The costly mistakes:
Adding dynamic timestamps to system prompts kills cache hit rates to zero Unstable JSON serialization with changing key orders silently breaks caching Any character change in prompt prefixes invalidates the entire cache The only way forward:
Keep prompt prefixes absolutely stable Make context append-only—never modify historical steps Ensure deterministic serialization Treat your context like a database index that needs optimization I’m seeing this firsthand in my own rent roll cleaning tool for senior living properties. The Excel analysis instructions stay stable in the prompt prefix, while only the actual property data changes. This append-only approach dramatically reduces costs compared to reconstructing the entire analytical framework for each file - even though each rent roll looks completely different to the LLM despite following similar patterns to human eyes.
2. Mask Tools, Don’t Remove Them When an agent’s tool library grows large, it gets “confused” and picks wrong tools. The natural instinct is to dynamically load only relevant tools.
Why this backfires:
Any change to tool definitions breaks KV-Cache for all subsequent requests When historical steps reference “deleted” tools, the model becomes completely confused The surgical approach: Use masking during decoding to constrain tool selection while keeping all tool definitions stable in context. Control the action space through logit masking, not context manipulation.
3. File System as Infinite Context Even 128K or 1M context windows get overwhelmed by a single webpage or PDF. Plus, model performance degrades in long contexts.
The breakthrough insight: Treat the file system as your ultimate context store. It’s infinite, persistent, and the agent can manipulate it directly. When content is too long, remove it from context but preserve the file path. This “recoverable compression” maintains access to information without permanent loss.
4. Use “Recitation” to Control Attention In complex tasks requiring 50+ tool calls, models easily drift from original goals due to the “lost-in-the-middle” problem.
The attention hack: Force the agent to create and continuously update a todo.md file. Each step requires rewriting this file, which effectively “recites” the global plan to the end of context, keeping core objectives in the model’s immediate attention span.
5. Keep Failures in Context When agents fail, our instinct is to clean up the “embarrassing” records and retry.
Why this is counterproductive: You’re paying for the model to repeat the same mistakes. Without failure context, it can’t learn from errors.
The learning approach: Preserve error messages, stack traces, and failed attempts as “observation results” in context. When the model sees “I tried A and failed with error X,” it can reflect and choose B instead.
The Meta-Lesson: Context Engineering is Experimental Science Perhaps the most important takeaway from the Manus experience is that context engineering is fundamentally experimental. We’re not trying to design perfect context upfront—we’re building systems that can evolve and improve their context management over time.
This means prioritizing adaptability over perfection, treating context as a “dynamic, learnable environment.” The REP Loop paradigm reinforces this: each iteration gives you data about what works and what doesn’t, enabling continuous refinement of your context engineering approach.
The future belongs to teams that master this experimental mindset, treating every agent interaction as a source of learning about better context design.

I had that sinking feeling during Anthropic’s product demo last week. You know the one—when you’re supposed to be the expert in the room, the person who knows Claude inside and out, but suddenly everything feels foreign.
The Anthropic team was walking through their enterprise offerings: Projects, Knowledge, the new Financial Services Analyst. Each feature seemed isolated, almost mundane when presented individually. Projects were just “workspaces to house user uploaded documents.” Knowledge was simply “parsing PDFs into markdown.” The Financial Services Analyst was just “MCP with enterprise support.”
I found myself nodding along, but internally struggling. This is it? This is what I’ve been raving about?
But then something clicked. Maybe it wasn’t about the individual components at all.
When Simple Parts Create Something Magical Later that day, I stumbled across a GitHub repository analyzing Claude Code’s internals—a reverse engineering effort that revealed something extraordinary hidden beneath the surface1. What I discovered made me realize why I had blanked out during the demo. I was looking at the trees instead of the forest.
Claude’s architecture isn’t impressive because of any single component. It’s impressive because of how these seemingly isolated parts combine to create emergent complexity.
Take Projects: on the surface, it’s just a workspace for documents. Knowledge appears to be simple PDF parsing. The Financial Services Analyst looks like basic MCP integration. Each component seems almost trivial when presented individually.
But then they presented “Deep Research,” and everything clicked. I was brought back from blanking out as I watched everything connect on top of this feature. Now the agent could tap into the project knowledge, search the internet, use MCP tools—finding everything useful to a research topic. Suddenly, those isolated components weren’t isolated anymore.
Here’s what I missed during the demo: these simple components complement each other perfectly. When combined with Sonnet’s dynamic planning capabilities, everything becomes possible. Projects provide the context, Knowledge gives the AI access to information, MCP connects to external systems, Deep Research orchestrates comprehensive analysis—and Sonnet conducts it all in real-time.
This is “Applied AI” at its finest. Instead of building specialized models for each use case, Anthropic is saying their base model is already good enough. They just need to explore the most out of it through intelligent architecture and tooling.
Why Are We Making This So Hard? The reverse engineering analysis revealed why Claude Code feels so effortless to use, despite being incredibly sophisticated under the hood. But it also made me question something that’s been bothering me for months in my day job.
I can’t count how many meetings I’ve sat through where colleagues debate RAG implementations, vector database architectures, and custom frameworks. “We need to build a knowledge base system,” they’ll say, then immediately dive into Pinecone vs. Weaviate, embedding models, chunking strategies, retrieval mechanisms. By the time we’re done planning, we’ve architected a system that would take months to build.
Meanwhile, Anthropic just says: “Upload your documents to Projects. Ask questions.” Done.
The Claude Code architecture is a masterclass in this philosophy. At its core, it runs on a multi-agent system with a 6-stage tool execution pipeline2. When you ask it to do something, it orchestrates an entire symphony of processes—agent loops, three-tier memory systems, intelligent compression algorithms that preserve 92% of key information, concurrency control that spawns up to 10 simultaneous sub-agents3.
But here’s the thing: you never see any of that complexity. You just get results.
This is what frustrates me about our approach to AI projects. We don’t have first-hand knowledge of LLM capabilities, yet we immediately jump to complex architectures. Why are we trapping ourselves in such heavy burdens when simple POC/MVP approaches seem so straightforward and easy with tools like Claude?
We’re planning two steps down the road when we haven’t even figured out step one. Meanwhile, Anthropic demonstrates that one powerful base model, enhanced by thoughtful architecture, can handle use cases we’re still debating how to build.
One Model vs. Many Models: A Philosophy Clash This architectural philosophy puts Anthropic in stark contrast with OpenAI’s approach. While OpenAI has proliferated models for every use case—GPT-4.1 for general tasks, GPT-4o for multimodal capabilities, o3-mini for reasoning, o4-mini-deep-research for research tasks, the new autonomous Codex agent for software engineering, DALL-E 3 for images, Whisper for audio—Anthropic doubles down on making one model incredibly versatile.
OpenAI’s strategy feels like the old software approach: build specialized tools for specialized tasks. Need image generation? Use DALL-E 3. Need autonomous coding? Use the new Codex agent. Need reasoning? Use o3-mini. Need deep research? Use o4-mini-deep-research. Need multimodal capabilities? Use GPT-4o. Each model is optimized for its domain, but the cognitive overhead of managing multiple models is significant.
Anthropic’s philosophy is fundamentally different: if your base model is good enough, you don’t need specialized variants. You need better architecture. Claude Code, Projects, Knowledge, Deep Research—they’re all powered by the same Sonnet and Opus models. The magic isn’t in having different models; it’s in having different ways to leverage the same powerful foundation.
This reminds me of Unix philosophy: “Do one thing and do it well.” But Anthropic flips it: “Do one thing incredibly well, then use elegant architecture to make it do everything else.”
The reverse engineering analysis shows this philosophy in action. Claude Code doesn’t succeed because it’s a specialized coding model—it succeeds because it’s Sonnet with an incredibly thoughtful multi-agent architecture, intelligent context management, and seamless tool integration.
From a business perspective, this is profound. Instead of training separate models for different enterprise use cases, Anthropic can focus on perfecting their base models and building better tooling around them. It’s more scalable, more maintainable, and frankly, more elegant.
The Power of Good Architecture That sinking feeling I had during the demo? It wasn’t because I didn’t know Claude’s features—I use them daily for 2-3 hours. It was because hearing someone else introduce tools I already knew made me think about them differently. I introduce these features to other people all the time, but this was the first time I actually heard them explained and thought about what they really were.
When you use something intuitively, you don’t think about its architecture. When you use Claude Code, you’re not thinking about the 6-stage tool execution pipeline or the intelligent compression algorithms. You’re just coding, and it works. When you use Deep Research, you’re not marveling at the multi-agent orchestration—you’re getting comprehensive insights seamlessly.
But hearing it described formally—“Projects are workspaces,” “Knowledge is PDF parsing,” “Financial Analyst is MCP with enterprise support”—suddenly made the magic visible. These weren’t separate features at all. They were carefully designed components of a unified system.
This is what great product design looks like: complexity that serves the user so well that it becomes invisible. But Anthropic doesn’t just hide complexity—they make human-in-the-loop interactions feel natural. Deep Research requires a button press that makes you think before the agent runs for 10-30 minutes. Extended Thinking is tucked away in option menus so users don’t accidentally enable it (and can be easily retired if the model gets smarter and no longer needs it).
The entire Anthropic experience feels unified and elegant—I’m running out of words for it. Anthropic could have built separate models for coding, research, document analysis, and financial services. Instead, they built one excellent model and surrounded it with thoughtful architecture.
The lesson for the rest of us building AI products? Maybe we should stop adding more models and start building better systems. Stop debating vector databases and start thinking about user experience. Stop planning two steps down the road and start building simple, elegant solutions that work today.
Because at the end of the day, users don’t care about your architecture—they care about results. And sometimes, the most sophisticated thing you can do is make complexity invisible.

Mark Zuckerberg is paying $100 million signing bonuses for AI researchers. Not $100,000—$100 million.1 And when you look at who Meta is hiring, a pattern emerges that reveals one of the most fascinating talent pipelines in modern technology.
Seven of Meta’s eleven publicly listed Superintelligence Labs recruits graduated from prestigious Chinese universities before pursuing advanced degrees in the US.2 Shengjia Zhao, Jiahui Yu, Shuchao Bi, Hongyu Ren—these aren’t just individual success stories. They represent a systematic phenomenon that’s reshaping the global AI landscape.
As someone who grew up in this educational system, I’ve been wondering: what exactly did China do right? And why does this talent pipeline seem so uniquely suited for AI dominance?
The answer lies in a perfect storm of three converging forces that created an unprecedented talent advantage—one that will continue shaping the AI race for decades to come.
The Numbers Don’t Lie The data is striking. Chinese researchers went from representing 29% of the world’s top AI experts in 2019 to 47% by 2022—nearly half of global AI talent.3 In 2024, China produces more AI research than the US, UK, and EU combined, with over 40% of global citation attention.4
This isn’t just about recent graduates. The current generation of AI leaders—those completing PhDs and joining companies like Meta, OpenAI, and Google—were shaped by China’s educational system during a very specific period: the late 1990s and early 2000s. Understanding what happened during those formative years reveals why Chinese talent is so sought-after today.
But this goes deeper than just educational outcomes. There are cultural and mathematical forces at play that most people don’t recognize—forces that created not just technical excellence, but exactly the kind of technical excellence that AI development demands.
The Educational Foundation: Building Systematic Thinkers To understand today’s AI talent pipeline, we need to look back at China’s educational system during the 1990s and early 2000s—the formative years for current AI leaders.
Mathematics as Core Infrastructure
Math wasn’t just a subject; it was one of three pillars (alongside Chinese and English) that every student had to master for the Gaokao college entrance exam. This wasn’t optional or tracked by ability—everyone, regardless of future career plans, spent years building deep mathematical foundations.
The results showed up in international assessments. Chinese students consistently dominated TIMSS scores, with some regions scoring 95+ points higher than Western countries.5 But this wasn’t just about test performance—it was about developing a particular kind of systematic thinking that translates directly to AI work.
Standardized Excellence
Unlike systems where educational quality varies dramatically by location or socioeconomic status, China’s curriculum was standardized nationwide. A student in rural Anhui province learned the same mathematical concepts, in the same sequence, as someone in Shanghai. This created consistency at scale—something unique in global education.
The Gaokao system, reinstated in 1977, created intense focus on mastery rather than exploration.6 Students spent years building foundational skills before specializing, developing what researchers call “delayed gratification” learning—exactly the patience required for the methodical work that AI development demands.
The STEM Pipeline
All students chose between Science (理科) and Humanities (文科) tracks in senior secondary school. The science track included physics, chemistry, and biology alongside advanced mathematics—creating a comprehensive STEM foundation that Western systems often lack.
This wasn’t about encouraging creativity or innovation in the Western sense. It was about building unshakeable technical foundations and systematic problem-solving skills. Students learned to work with complex, multi-step problems and to persist through difficulties—skills that translate directly to training neural networks and debugging AI systems.
The Cultural Edge: Accepting Brilliance Without Social Polish Here’s where the story gets interesting, and where my perspective as someone who grew up in this system might offer unique insight.
Collective Benefit Over Individual Charm
Chinese culture has a fundamentally different relationship with intellectual brilliance, especially when it comes with social awkwardness. Research shows that Chinese culture views intelligence as “reflecting wisdom and desire to improve society as a whole rather than only themselves”—quite different from Western emphasis on individual achievement.7
In China, if you contribute technical value, social awkwardness is not just tolerated—it’s often expected. There’s “high appreciation for official titles and positions” based on intellectual achievement. A brilliant but socially clumsy mathematician or engineer gains respect through their technical contributions, not their networking ability.
Protection Through Hierarchy
The cultural emphasis on “thinking before you speak” and “showing respect for those higher in hierarchy” actually protects intellectually gifted but socially awkward individuals. Unlike Western systems where networking and presentation skills often matter as much as technical ability, Chinese academic and professional environments create space for pure technical contributors.
Group Success Over Individual Polish
In China, “any success is regarded as success for the company, family, or team.”8 If your algorithm works, if your research produces results, if your code solves the problem—that’s what matters. Personal charisma becomes secondary to technical contribution.
This creates a cultural safety net for the kinds of minds that AI development needs: people who can spend months debugging neural network architectures, who obsess over mathematical elegance, who prefer precise technical discussion to small talk.
The Population Mathematics Advantage But there’s another factor that amplifies everything else: pure numbers.
The Scale Advantage
With 1.4 billion people, even identical rates of exceptional talent would give China a 4x advantage over the United States. If one in 10,000 people has the specific cognitive profile ideal for AI research, that translates to:
140,000 potential AI talents in China 33,000 in the United States 6,700 in the United Kingdom But the rates aren’t identical—they’re skewed by the educational and cultural factors we’ve discussed.
Statistical Inevitability
When you combine China’s mathematical education foundation with cultural acceptance of technical brilliance and massive population scale, you get what statisticians would call an inevitability. China doesn’t need to be better at producing AI talent per capita—though evidence suggests it is—it just needs to be competitive while having four times the base population.
The Golden Generation
Current AI leaders represent what might be called China’s “golden generation”—people educated during the peak of this educational system, before demographic decline, but after educational investment had reached scale. They benefited from both systematic mathematical training and the cultural values that support technical excellence.
The Perfect Symbiosis: Foundation Meets Innovation The real insight isn’t that Chinese education is universally superior, but that it produces exactly what the AI field needs when combined with American research infrastructure.
What Chinese Students Bring
Unshakeable mathematical foundations Systematic problem-solving approaches High tolerance for difficult, sustained technical work Comfort with hierarchy and technical mentorship Cultural acceptance of prioritizing technical excellence over social skills What the US System Provides
Massive research funding ($430 billion annually in R&D)9 Freedom to explore novel approaches and take intellectual risks Collaborative networks with top researchers worldwide Pathways from research to commercial application Venture capital ecosystem supporting translation to products The Result Chinese foundational rigor + American innovation capital + research freedom = today’s AI breakthroughs. It’s not coincidental that so many current AI advances come from Chinese-educated researchers working in American institutions.
Looking Forward: The Talent Wars Intensify This pipeline advantage won’t last forever, but it will persist longer than most people expect.
The Immediate Crisis
The AI talent shortage is already severe. Globally, there’s a 50% AI talent gap in 2024.10 The US needs 1.3 million AI workers but can only fill 645,000 positions.11 China faces its own crunch: needing 6 million AI workers by 2030 but universities only producing 2 million.12
This scarcity is driving unprecedented recruitment strategies. Companies are already recruiting high school students through programs at Microsoft, NASA, MIT, and Stanford.13 The UAE is offering $1 million+ annually to lure researchers.14 Twenty-four countries have launched startup visa programs specifically targeting US-trained AI talent.15
China’s Remaining Advantage
Despite population decline, China retains a significant advantage. The country has been losing population since 2022, but today’s 20-year-olds—born during peak population in 2004—will be prime AI researchers through the 2050s.16 This gives China a 30-year runway of talent advantage from their “last golden generation.”
The New Reality
We’re entering an era where AI talent is treated as a national resource, where governments recruit researchers like they once recruited nuclear physicists. Companies that wait for traditional university graduation will lose to those recruiting earlier and more globally.
The perfect storm that created China’s AI talent pipeline was historically unique—a combination of systematic education, cultural values, and population scale that may never be replicated. But its effects will shape the global AI landscape for decades to come.
Understanding this pipeline isn’t just about explaining current hiring patterns. It’s about recognizing how educational philosophies, cultural values, and demographic realities combine to create competitive advantages that persist across generations. The next time you see a $100 million signing bonus for an AI researcher, you’ll know you’re witnessing the culmination of forces set in motion decades ago.

I stumbled across Calvin French-Owen’s reflections on his time at OpenAI and found myself completely absorbed—not by the high-level insights about AI safety or AGI timelines, but by the operational details buried throughout. The kind of specifics that make you go “wait, they did what in 7 weeks?”
There’s something deeply fascinating about getting a peek behind the curtain of a company operating at the technological frontier. Calvin’s post is full of these moments where you realize just how different building products looks when you have the resources, talent, and mandate to try audacious things from scratch.
Here are the details that stuck with me, and why they make me a little envious of what it must feel like to build without constraints.
The Monorepo Reality “Giant Python monorepo” is such a delightfully specific detail. In most companies, suggesting a monorepo triggers debates about build times, dependency management, and team autonomy. At OpenAI? They just… do it. And apparently live with CI that takes 30 minutes to run on master and “frequently breaks.”
This feels like the engineering equivalent of luxury problems. Yes, your builds are slow and your CI is fragile, but you’re also shipping frontier AI models. The tolerance for technical debt when you’re racing toward AGI is apparently quite high—and honestly, that’s probably the right trade-off.
The infrastructure choices are equally fascinating: everything on Azure, FastAPI for APIs, Pydantic for validation. Nothing exotic or cutting-edge, just solid, boring choices that let you focus on the hard problems. There’s wisdom in not reinventing wheels when you’re already reinventing intelligence.
Speed vs. Scale Tensions The Codex story is wild: 7 weeks from start to launch with a team of about 17 people (8 engineers, 4 researchers, 2 designers, 2 GTM, 1 PM). Seven weeks! And it generated 630,000 public PRs in the first 53 days.
But then Calvin also mentions the challenge of scaling from 1,000 to 3,000 employees in a single year. That’s a fascinating tension—you can still move incredibly fast on individual products, but the organizational overhead is crushing you in other ways.
Most companies optimize for predictable scaling. OpenAI seems to optimize for breakthrough speed while accepting the chaos that rapid growth brings. Slack replacing email entirely, highly fluid team structures, rapid direction changes—it sounds simultaneously thrilling and exhausting.
The Stack That Ships The technical details scattered throughout are fascinating. They built their own reimplementation of Meta’s TAO graph database. They created custom container runtimes and repo downloading optimizations for Codex. They fine-tuned models specifically for code editing.
This is what “build vs. buy” looks like when you have the talent pipeline from Meta and the resources to solve problems from first principles. Most companies would integrate an existing graph database or use off-the-shelf container solutions. OpenAI just… builds their own.
There’s something both admirable and absurd about this level of custom engineering. It’s the kind of technical ambition that only makes sense when you’re well-funded and operating at the frontier.
The Meta Pipeline One detail that caught my attention: the “significant Meta → OpenAI engineering talent pipeline.” This isn’t just about hiring good engineers—it’s about importing institutional knowledge and technical DNA.
When you poach enough talent from one place, you don’t just get their skills, you get their approaches, their tools, their assumptions about how things should be built. The TAO graph database reimplementation suddenly makes more sense in this context. It’s not just “we need a graph database,” it’s “we know how Meta solved this problem, and we can do it better.”
This kind of talent concentration is fascinating from a product development perspective. Most companies have to learn hard lessons the slow way. OpenAI gets to inherit lessons already learned elsewhere and apply them to novel problems.
Product Velocity Envy Here’s what really gets me: “GPU cost is a major consideration for every feature.” What a luxury problem to have! Most product teams are constrained by engineering time, user research timelines, or market positioning. OpenAI’s constraint is that their compute is so expensive they have to think carefully about what’s worth the GPU cycles.
This fundamentally changes how you approach product development. When your marginal cost per experiment is measured in thousands of dollars of compute, you probably get very good at hypothesizing, very disciplined about testing, and very focused on high-impact features.
Compare this to the typical startup approach of “throw spaghetti at the wall and see what sticks.” When spaghetti costs $10,000 per throw, you develop much better aim.
What This Makes Me Think About Reading Calvin’s reflections, I keep coming back to one feeling: envy for the freedom to build things ground-up with proper resources and the organizational mandate to take big swings.
Most product development happens within constraints—legacy systems, technical debt, budget limitations, risk-averse stakeholders. You optimize for incremental improvements because that’s what’s feasible.
But what would it feel like to work somewhere with the resources and audacity to say “let’s reimplement TAO” or “let’s ship an AI coding assistant in 7 weeks”? Where the constraint isn’t “can we afford to try this?” but “is this the best use of our expensive compute?”
There’s something deeply appealing about that level of ambition, even if it comes with 30-minute CI builds and the chaos of hypergrowth. Sometimes I wonder what products we’d all build if we had OpenAI’s combination of resources, talent, and willingness to bet big on uncertain outcomes.
Calvin’s full post is worth reading for the cultural and strategic insights too, but these operational details were what caught my product manager brain. Sometimes the most interesting part of any story is simply how the sausage gets made.

Translation Note: This is a translation of the original Chinese blog post “写在 Kimi K2 发布之后：再也不仅仅是 ChatBot” by Justin Wong (bigeagle), published on July 13, 2025. All opinions expressed are those of the original author.
Introduction Two days ago, the Kimi K2 we’d been working on for most of the year was finally released. After pulling an all-nighter before launch, I slept soundly for two days and finally have some time to write about my thoughts.
Disclaimer: Everything below represents my personal views and does not represent the company’s position.
Additional disclaimer: Everything below is handcrafted the old-fashioned way (only using GitHub Copilot as an advanced input method).
About “Frontend Development” Since Claude 3.5 Sonnet, AI frontend development has reached a practically usable level. Almost all new models since then have showcased their frontend development capabilities, and Kimi K2 is no exception. Here, I’d like to share my personal thoughts on this.
Text-based AI has always defaulted to outputting Markdown, and products have been essentially advanced ChatBots. People’s expectations of a ChatBot are nothing more than answering questions, writing articles, and providing emotional value like a human would. Once I saw user feedback requesting that Kimi “reformat the article to fit on one A4 page” - this was obviously impossible in pure text mode, and I dismissed this case as a joke between product managers and programmers.
Around March of this year, when Kimi Researcher was being developed, both OpenAI and Gemini’s Deep Research ultimately delivered pure text research reports. We thought we could do something different by leveraging the already decent frontend programming capabilities at the time, giving users a richer, more interactive final report. The final form of this idea was revealed to the public after Kimi Researcher went live and received quite positive feedback.
But when I saw this idea, something completely different flashed through my mind: no one dictates that text AI must output markdown. If “frontend programming” becomes AI’s default interaction method, what would the product form become?
From “chat-first” to “artifact-first.” Users wouldn’t need to engage in lengthy conversations with AI to get what they want. Instead, they could directly tell AI what interactive application they need, and AI would create it for them. This fundamentally changes the user’s interaction paradigm with AI.
For example, instead of asking “help me analyze this data,” users could say “create an interactive dashboard for me to analyze this data.” Instead of asking “help me write a report,” they could say “create an interactive report generator for me.” This is no longer just a ChatBot - it’s an intelligent application generator.
About Tool Use & Agent At the beginning of the year, MCP started gaining popularity, and we thought about whether we could also connect Kimi to various third-party tools through MCP. At that time, we achieved quite good results through RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) during K1.5 development, so we thought we could replicate this approach - get a bunch of real MCP servers and directly integrate them into the RL environment for joint training.
This approach quickly hit a wall. First, deployment was troublesome - for example, Blender MCP is easy for users who already have Blender, but installing Blender in the RL environment becomes a burden. Second, and more fatally, many third-party tools require login to use. You can’t just register a bunch of Notion accounts for training Notion MCP usage, right?
But we changed our perspective. My hypothesis is: the model already knows how to use tools from pretraining; we just need to activate this capability. The foundation of this hypothesis is easy to understand: pretraining has seen massive amounts of code data, including numerous API calls in various languages and expressions. If we treat each API call as a tool, then the model should already know how to use them. Another foundation is that pretrained models already master rich world knowledge - for example, if you ask it to roleplay a Linux Terminal, it can interact with you quite convincingly. So obviously, for terminal tool calls, only a small amount of data should be needed to activate this capability.
Therefore, we designed a rather elegant workflow:
Simulation Phase: Use the model to simulate tool behavior instead of connecting to real tools Activation Phase: Use minimal real data to activate the capability that already exists in the model Refinement Phase: Fine-tune based on actual usage patterns This approach avoids the complexity of real tool integration while leveraging the model’s existing knowledge. The key insight is that the model doesn’t need to learn how to use tools from scratch - it needs to learn how to activate and apply the knowledge it already has.
Why Open Source First, to gain some fame. If K2 was just a closed-source service, it wouldn’t have received as much attention and discussion.
Second, to leverage community strength in improving the technical ecosystem. Within 24 hours of open-sourcing, the community had already created MLX implementations and 4-bit quantization - things our small team couldn’t accomplish alone.
Most importantly: Open source means higher technical standards, which will force us to create better models, more aligned with AGI goals.
This isn’t just about releasing model weights. Open-sourcing means the first-party can no longer use “hack” methods to artificially enhance results. We must produce a truly universal model that any third party can easily reproduce.
For closed-source chatbots, users don’t know the underlying workflow or model complexity. I’ve heard rumors of services using dozens of models and hundreds of scenario classifications - this approach is contrary to true AGI development.
By open-sourcing, we prevent taking shortcuts and ensure a more rigorous approach to model development. I even playfully told the product team that if someone creates a more interesting application using Kimi K2, I’ll challenge them on it.
About Determination and Some Potentially Controversial Scattered Views Despite criticism about our previous large-scale marketing efforts, Kimi stopped investing in marketing. Even when “Kimi” disappeared from app store search results, we did not resume marketing campaigns.
I believe “hard capabilities are the best promotion” - if the model is good, it will gain market recognition. I see pursuing AGI as an “extremely perilous path” that requires total commitment. Hesitation will definitely lead to failure in the pursuit of AGI.
I’m critical of purely application-focused AI strategies. Most Agent products are insignificant without advanced foundational models. I’m skeptical of approaches that prioritize Return on Investment (ROI) over technological advancement.
Our core motivation is pushing the upper limits of intelligence through model development. We’re willing to make radical organizational decisions to pursue AGI goals. I believe the model’s intelligence fundamentally determines an AI system’s capabilities.
This is an uncompromising approach to AI development, prioritizing technological advancement over short-term market gains. We’re committed to this path despite its risks and challenges.
Conclusion I know Kimi K2 still has countless flaws. Now more than ever, I want K3.
Addendum I didn’t expect this article to attract so much attention (scared). I must admit that while my sharp criticism was satisfying to write, some of my statements were too extreme. I have great respect for the entire industry - entrepreneurship is not easy, and we are all fellow travelers on the path to AGI.

Note: This is a translation of the original Chinese article by grapeot, published on July 12, 2025. The original article can be found at: https://yage.ai/kimi-k2.html
Recently, whenever a new large language model is released, we can always see a wave of evaluation reports. But there’s an interesting phenomenon: the vast majority of evaluations are invariably confined to an environment we’re most familiar with—the chat interface.
This is actually a fundamental limitation. In 2025, when Agentic AI is all the rage, evaluating a model designed for Agentic capabilities within a chat interface is like using whiteboard coding to interview a development director. The feedback you get has almost no relation to its core capabilities.
Kimi K2, released by Moonshot AI, has from the very beginning clearly positioned Agentic capabilities—that is, the ability for intelligent agents to autonomously use tools to complete tasks—in an extremely important position. This is a very rare choice in the entire field. For example, DeepSeek R1 only added tool-calling functionality quite some time after its release, and many platforms like ollama still don’t fully support it today. Kimi K2 takes the opposite approach, developing Agentic capabilities as a core competency, which in itself is worth evaluating with a paradigm that’s closer to its design goals.
Why We Must Go Beyond Chat Interfaces: The Evaluation Dilemma of Agentic AI But before we proceed, we must first clarify the premise of our discussion: What exactly is the core of Agentic AI? It has two inseparable core elements:
Autonomous Decision-Making and Feedback Loops: This is the true manifestation of intelligence. An Agentic model doesn’t just passively answer questions; it needs to be able to autonomously break down a large goal into step-by-step action plans. More critically, it observes the results of its own actions—such as whether a file was successfully written or code compilation failed—and then adjusts based on this feedback to decide what to do next. This is a continuous perception-thinking-action loop.
Tool Invocation and Environment Interaction: These are the “hands and feet” connecting the model’s brain to the real world. The model itself cannot directly operate your computer; it needs to achieve this through tool invocation. These tools can be operating system-level functions, such as reading and writing files or executing code, or they can be functions that connect to the external world, such as web searches or retrieving video content.
Understanding these two points helps us see why simply chatting with AI completely fails to evaluate its Agentic capabilities.
First, the chat format, in most cases, doesn’t require invoking any tools at all, so naturally it cannot evaluate this capability. Its interaction is purely text generation. You ask, it answers, rather than you speak, it acts. Here we are in 2025, still using the same approach to evaluate ChatGPT to assess a model designed for Agentic purposes—this itself represents a disconnect.
Second, chat interfaces severely limit the complexity of problems. A true Agentic task requires continuous context and environmental awareness. Tasks within chat interfaces are often isolated with extremely short contexts. They cannot construct the kind of feedback loop mentioned earlier, where the results of a previous compilation failure determine the next round of modification strategies.
Therefore, the only way to evaluate the true capabilities of an Agentic model is to place it in a real environment where it can get its hands dirty. I spent some time conducting a more systematic analysis of Kimi K2 that’s closer to its design intentions, by directly writing code to call its API.
Programming Test: The Friction Between High-Level Intelligence and Execution In the Agentic world, programming is a classic comprehensive task. To evaluate a model’s true capabilities in programming tasks, we similarly cannot adopt the mode of copying and pasting code back and forth in chat interfaces. That question-and-answer approach fragments what should be a continuous, complex engineering task into countless discrete, scattered Q&As. This way of using AI is like applying telegraph thinking to sending WeChat messages: compressing what should be an immersive collaborative information space into a small box where context is frequently lost, then making do with manual补全 to keep things running—both inefficient and counterproductive.
This is precisely why the emergence of Agentic programming environments like Cursor or Claude Code represents revolutionary progress.
Their core value lies in building a real arena where AI models can truly stretch their legs. In this environment, the model is no longer just a chat partner, but transforms into a copilot equipped with a series of tools like reading and writing files, executing code. It can finally work like a real human developer in actual codebases, building that crucial feedback loop and truly participating in stateful, continuous task flows.
Therefore, to evaluate K2’s real capabilities, the first thing I did was integrate it into the powerful Agentic programming environment of Claude Code (specific methods at the end of the article), and had it develop a chicken-crossing-the-road game from scratch. (Below is a video of the game it created)
Watch the chicken-crossing-the-road game video here.
The first version it produced was quite playable, and after two or three iterations, it was basically bug-free. However, the entire development process was far from smooth—it could even be described as bumpy. I had a clear impression: there exists an obvious gap between the model’s high-level intelligence and low-level tool execution.
On one hand, Kimi K2’s intelligence is first-rate. Its understanding of tasks, decomposition of game logic, and the quality of final code generation are all at industry-leading levels. It can understand my intentions well and write genuinely effective programs or perform effective debugging. This is a very smart “brain.”
But on the other hand, when this brain needs to interact with the real file system through its “hands and feet” (i.e., tool calls), systematic friction begins to appear. For example, in the Claude Code environment, it seems to have its own preferences for handling file paths, which causes it to repeatedly fail when attempting to read and write files. Those “cannot find string to replace” errors in the logs are not random bugs, but rather a consistent pattern throughout. This gives me the feeling that the model and tools are like speaking the same language with different accents, often leading to misunderstandings.
More seriously, when it’s handling particularly complex tasks, it sometimes just stops mid-sentence. This sudden interruption of the reasoning process is fatal for an Agentic system. An intelligent agent that cannot reliably complete tasks is unreliable. So what might be the root causes of these problems? I speculate there are mainly two levels of reasons:
First is systematic tool mismatch. Claude Code is an environment Anthropic built specifically for their own Claude models. Its tool instruction formats, internal prompt templates, and expectations for model outputs have all been fine-tuned to perfectly match Claude models’ temperament and personality (universal Agentic programming tools like Cursor or Trae also need individual adaptation for each model. The main reason we don’t use Cursor/Trae here is that they don’t have the convenient integration method like Claude Code Router). Kimi K2 is like a potentially highly skilled actor with a different accent who’s suddenly placed in a script written for another lead actor. It can understand the general meaning of the lines, but consistently deviates on certain key intonations, rhythms, and subtexts. The file path handling issues mentioned earlier are likely manifestations of this accent mismatch.
Second, a more specific technical reason might be context window limitations. Agentic programming environments are very context-intensive, requiring the entire conversation history, system prompts, and code from multiple currently open files to be stuffed into the model’s memory. Claude Code’s natively adapted Claude 4 model has a 200K context window, while Kimi K2’s currently available API is 128K. When the entire task context exceeds this length, the model may exhibit unpredictable behavior, such as the sudden reasoning interruptions I observed. This might not be Kimi forgetting what to say, but rather its workbench being full and unable to process new information. Of course, this is just one possibility; another possibility is that, similar to Gemini 2.5 Pro, Kimi K2’s training process didn’t perfectly handle long-chain tool processing, which would require further in-depth investigation.
Therefore, my hypothesis is that the bumpy development process is not due to deficiencies in Kimi K2’s intelligence level. It exposes a deeper problem: the contradiction between a potentially top-tier AI brain and hands and feet that haven’t been fully adapted to it. This results in a less-than-ideal user experience. This is a problem worth considering for all teams dedicated to Agentic AI development.
Information Research: The Execution Resilience of Agentic Models My second test was open-ended information research. This is a scenario that better tests a model’s autonomous planning and iterative execution capabilities.
It was precisely in this test that Kimi K2 demonstrated its enormous value as a system component. I discovered it has a very precious characteristic that I call task execution resilience. When facing a complex research topic, it will very naturally generate large quantities of diverse keywords, then tirelessly conduct multiple rounds of iterative searches. It has a strong bias for action, while many other models, when facing this type of open task, quickly start to slack off, preferring to use their existing knowledge rather than actively explore. For example, GPT-4o, Gemini, Deepseek, and Qwen all have similar problems. Even when the system prompt repeatedly emphasizes “please absolutely must search with multiple keywords,” they’ll just casually search for one or two rounds or even be too lazy to search at all and directly start answering.
Of course, it also has a significant shortcoming. Possibly because K2 is not a reasoning model, while it’s very good at collecting and compiling information and can provide you with an extremely detailed list of materials, it’s not good at extracting profound, high-level insights from these materials. It’s more like a top-tier information gatherer rather than an analyst. This point is actually very similar to o3—o3 can also tirelessly invoke multiple rounds of searches, but in the end often just generates a simple running list. Moreover, this issue of thinking depth is very difficult to change. It’s like telling an intern multiple times (through prompts) that reports need strategic height—they still can’t write VP-level reports for you. This is a limitation of the model’s inherent capabilities.
But this can already provide tremendous value. A model with strong execution resilience is the foundation for building complex Agentic systems. Because in a system, the most valuable quality is not occasional flashes of brilliance, but predictable, reliable execution. A component that can always faithfully complete instructions is far more valuable than one that’s brilliant but makes its own decisions. You can build more diverse and reliable automated workflows around it. I used to always use o3 to complete such tasks, but due to o3’s cost, I was always hesitant to extend this approach to more complex tasks. Now Kimi K2’s emergence has given me a low-cost but quite comparable quality option.
This directly spawned a very efficient workflow. I now use Kimi K2 as the frontend of a research system, leveraging its strong execution resilience and long-text capabilities to perform carpet-bombing information gathering on any topic I want to research. Then, I hand the extremely information-rich context that Kimi has organized directly to a reasoning model that excels at deep analysis, such as Gemini 2.5 Pro as the backend, letting it complete the final step of analysis and insight extraction. This two-stage combination works surprisingly well. Not only does the final output quality far exceed any single model, but due to Kimi’s cost-effectiveness, the entire process costs significantly less compared to o3. This gives me a clear view of Kimi K2’s precise positioning in a complex Agentic system: a tireless, exceptionally capable doer.
Here’s an example:
Inference process
Moreover, I’ve found that Kimi’s shortcoming in reasoning ability can also be compensated through workflow design. I’ll have it first play the role of an architect, generating a detailed and clear step-by-step plan for a complex task. This plan itself is equivalent to us manually injecting a thinking component for it, externalizing and structuring the thinking process. Then, I’ll have it play the role of a scheduler, strictly and step-by-step calling various tools to execute the plan it just created. This achieves a decoupling of planning and execution in a multi-agent system. As a scheduler, it can call search engines, invoke code interpreters, and even call another model that excels at analysis (such as Gemini 2.5 Pro) to complete a particular step in the plan that requires deep thinking.
Some Final Thoughts So, after this round of testing, I feel that Kimi K2’s advantages and deficiencies are both quite apparent. Its strategic bet on the Agentic direction is a rather visionary move. But between its powerful potential and current reliable execution capability, there indeed still exists a gap.
Kimi K2’s most precious asset is its intelligent brain. But the value of this core asset is being consumed by unstable tool calls and ecosystem friction. If we want it to fully realize its potential, I think there are two things that may be unavoidable:
First is proactively solving the last-mile problems of the ecosystem. Expecting the community to spontaneously create perfect adaptations for Kimi would be a very lengthy process. A more proactive approach would be to directly engage in deep collaboration with one or two mainstream Agentic programming tools, such as Cursor or Trae, for targeted fine-tuning, or even releasing official, deeply adapted open-source toolchains. There’s only one goal: upgrading the usability of Agentic capabilities to the reliability that developers can trust. This is a key step in building a true moat.
Second is treating reasoning stability as a core engineering metric. The problem of tool calls stopping midway must be located and solved at its root. Because this problem directly determines whether Kimi K2 will ultimately become an interesting toy or a productivity tool that developers can rely on. The upper limit of an intelligent agent is often determined by its most unstable component.
Overall, Kimi K2 gives me the feeling of unpolished rough jade. Its core material—the model’s intelligence—is excellent, showing us the enormous possibilities of Agentic AI’s future. Its task completion resilience and cost-effectiveness have already made it the default frontend of my information research system. But the challenges it currently faces are not a lack of intelligence, but rather the friction between engineering and ecosystem integration. What position it will ultimately occupy in AI history will largely depend on the determination and speed of bridging this gap.

The Disconnect “I honestly don’t see the productivity gains everyone’s talking about,” my tech lead said during our weekly one-on-one. We’d been discussing our team’s AI tool adoption, and I had just mentioned how Claude Code had transformed my workflow. “It takes me longer to review the AI-generated code than to just write it myself.”
My coder friend echoed this sentiment over coffee a few days later: “I mean, it’s helpful for boilerplate stuff, but for anything complex? I spend more time explaining the context than it would take to just solve it.”
Meanwhile, I’m over here feeling like I’ve gained a superpower. Claude helps me draft technical specs, brainstorm user research questions, validate market assumptions, prototype features—the list goes on. Some days, it feels like having a brilliant intern who never gets tired and can context-switch between business strategy and technical implementation seamlessly.
What’s going on here? Are we just experiencing different tools, or is something deeper happening?
The Research Reality Check Then I stumbled across a study that stopped me in my tracks. METR (formerly ARC Evals) published research showing that experienced developers using AI tools actually took 19% longer to complete tasks than those working without AI assistance.1
Read that again: 19% slower.
But here’s the kicker—despite being measurably slower, these developers believed AI had made them 20% more productive. Even after experiencing the slowdown firsthand.
The perception-reality gap is staggering. And it perfectly captures the tension I was seeing in my own team.
The Wrong Question My first instinct was to frame this as a role-based problem: “Why do product managers see AI productivity gains while developers don’t?”
But the more I thought about it, the more I realized I was asking the wrong question.
The real question isn’t about roles. It’s about something much more fundamental: What drives some people to successfully expand their capabilities with AI while others struggle?
Because when I look at my own AI usage, it’s not really about being a product manager. It’s about something else entirely.
The Agency Factor Here’s what I think is actually happening: effective AI usage requires agency and curiosity—a genuine desire to expand beyond your current boundaries.
With LLMs, I can stretch my capabilities in two directions simultaneously:
Toward Users: I use Claude to generate user interview scripts, analyze survey responses, simulate customer conversations, and brainstorm edge cases I might miss. It’s like having access to a research team that never sleeps.
Toward Technical: I use Claude Code to build POCs, understand system architectures, and create functional prototypes that illustrate my ideas to the engineering team. Last week, I built a working dashboard mockup in React—something that would have required a week of back-and-forth with our frontend team to communicate.
From a value chain perspective, I’m constantly using LLMs to expand my business knowledge through ongoing conversations about market dynamics, competitive analysis, and strategic frameworks. It’s like having a consultant available 24/7 who’s read every business book and can help me think through complex problems.
But here’s the key insight: you have to actually enjoy learning to initiate these actions.
The Learning Enjoyment Prerequisite I don’t want this to sound condescending, because I’m genuinely curious about understanding where my own passion comes from. But I think there’s something about intrinsic motivation that determines AI productivity outcomes.
When I see a technical challenge, my immediate response is: “How can I understand this well enough to contribute meaningfully?” When I encounter a user problem, I think: “What context am I missing, and how can I gather it quickly?”
This isn’t because I’m a product manager—it’s because I’m genuinely curious about expanding my capabilities. The AI tools just happen to make that expansion possible in ways that weren’t feasible before.
My tech lead, on the other hand, is incredibly skilled at what he does. He can architect complex systems and solve challenging technical problems with elegance and efficiency. But he’s not necessarily driven to expand into product strategy or user research—and that’s perfectly fine. In fact, his deep technical expertise is exactly what our team needs.
The difference isn’t competence—it’s motivation direction.
Why This Manifests Differently Across Roles This curiosity-driven approach to AI might appear more beneficial for product managers, but I think that’s correlation, not causation. Product management, by nature, requires constant context switching and boundary spanning. We’re used to being “good enough” at many things rather than excellent at one thing.
This orientation happens to align well with how LLMs work best—they’re generalists that can help with a wide variety of tasks, but they need human expertise to guide them toward quality outcomes.
Developers, especially senior ones, often have the opposite orientation: deep expertise in specific domains. When you’re already excellent at something, AI assistance can feel like more overhead than benefit. Why use a tool that gives you 80% of what you could produce at 100% quality?
But I’ve seen developers who approach AI with the same curiosity-driven mindset I described, and they see similar productivity gains. They use AI to explore new languages, understand unfamiliar codebases, generate test cases, and explain complex concepts to stakeholders. The common thread isn’t their role—it’s their approach to expanding capabilities.
The Meta-Question This brings me to a question I’ve been wrestling with: Where does this drive to expand actually come from?
I catch myself using AI to learn about topics I’ll probably never use professionally—diving into urban planning principles when discussing feature adoption curves, or exploring cognitive psychology when thinking about user interface design. There’s something inherently satisfying about connecting disparate domains, and AI makes that kind of intellectual wandering both possible and productive.
Is this just personality? Is it learned behavior from years of product management, where you’re constantly the person who needs to understand “enough” about everything to facilitate good decisions? Or is it something else entirely?
I don’t have a complete answer, but I suspect it’s related to what I wrote about in my first post—the conscious effort to think deliberately rather than defaulting to automation. AI becomes incredibly powerful when you combine it with intentional learning, but it requires you to actively choose expansion over efficiency.
What This Means for Teams Understanding this dynamic has practical implications for how we think about AI adoption in organizations.
Instead of focusing on role-based AI training (“Here’s how PMs should use AI, here’s how developers should use AI”), maybe we should focus on curiosity cultivation. How do we create environments where people feel safe to experiment with expanding their capabilities? How do we reward learning and boundary-crossing, not just execution?
The developers who struggle with AI productivity aren’t struggling because they’re developers—they’re struggling because they’re being asked to adopt tools that require a different kind of motivation than the one that made them excellent at their current role.
The product managers who see huge gains aren’t succeeding because they’re PMs—they’re succeeding because they’re approaching AI with a learning mindset that happens to align with how these tools work best.
The Bigger Pattern This connects back to the themes I’ve been exploring in previous posts about context engineering and conscious effort. AI productivity isn’t just about the tools—it’s about the intentional work of expanding your own capabilities and staying curious about domains beyond your core expertise.
The conscious effort isn’t about resisting automation—it’s about using automation to become more capable, more curious, and ultimately more valuable in an AI-augmented world.
Maybe the real AI productivity paradox isn’t about roles at all. Maybe it’s about the difference between people who use AI to become more of what they already are versus people who use AI to become more than what they thought possible.

Opening “The downside of using deep research is that we can’t control the credibility of the sources, and it could lead to heavy hallucination.”
My tech lead paused after saying this during our POC discussion. We were debating whether to integrate OpenAI’s new deep research models—o3-deep-research and o4-mini-deep-research—into our product, and the conversation had taken that familiar turn—the one where everyone nods knowingly about “hallucinations” without really understanding what’s happening under the hood.
After some back-and-forth, we agreed the solution was “setting expectations with users.” Classic product management: when you can’t solve the technical problem, manage the human problem.
But as I walked away from that meeting, I remembered reading something from Anthropic about hallucinations that challenged my assumptions. That evening, I fell into a rabbit hole of research papers and blog posts, chasing a simple question that had been nagging at me:
If LLMs work like humans, why can humans confidently say “I don’t know” but LLMs seem to struggle with it?
What I discovered was both more fascinating and more practical than I expected.
What Anthropic Actually Found Here’s where things get interesting. I expected to find research about making LLMs smarter or more cautious. Instead, Anthropic’s 2025 research revealed something counter-intuitive: Claude’s default behavior is actually to decline answering questions.1
Let me repeat that: the model’s natural inclination is to not answer.
According to their paper “Tracing the thoughts of a large language model,” Claude has internal neural circuits that act like a decision-making system. Think of it as an internal debate: “Do I know enough about this to respond, or should I stay quiet?”
The researchers found that Claude only answers questions when something actively inhibits this default reluctance. It’s like having a naturally shy person who only speaks up when they’re really confident about something.
So if that’s the case, why do we still get hallucinations?
The circuit misfires.
Through intervention experiments, Anthropic could artificially activate the “known answer” features in Claude’s neural network. When they did this, they could make the model consistently hallucinate that “Michael Batkin plays chess” (a fictional fact). Sometimes, this sort of “misfire” happens naturally, without any intervention—and that’s when we get hallucinations.
It’s not that the model is trying to be helpful by making things up. It’s that the internal system responsible for saying “I don’t know” occasionally gets it wrong and thinks it knows something it doesn’t.
This discovery flipped my understanding completely. The problem isn’t that LLMs are too eager to answer—it’s that their internal “should I answer this?” mechanism sometimes malfunctions.
The Fundamental Difference: Human vs. LLM “Hallucination” But this raised an even bigger question for me: if LLMs have mechanisms similar to humans for deciding when to speak, why do humans seem so much better at saying “I don’t know”?
The answer lies in a fundamental misunderstanding of what’s actually happening when LLMs “hallucinate.”
It’s Not Really Hallucination Cognitive scientists have been pushing back on the term “hallucination” for LLMs. In humans, hallucination involves perceiving things that aren’t there—seeing, hearing, or feeling something that doesn’t exist in reality. But LLMs don’t perceive anything. They don’t have sensory experiences.
A more accurate term might be “confabulation”—when someone fills in gaps in their memory with plausible but false information.2 This happens to humans too, but the underlying mechanisms are completely different.
System 1 vs. System 2 Thinking Remember Daniel Kahneman’s “Thinking, Fast and Slow”? He describes two modes of human cognition:
System 1: Fast, automatic, intuitive responses System 2: Slow, deliberate, analytical thinking When humans say “I don’t know,” we’re often engaging System 2—we pause, reflect on our knowledge, and make a conscious decision about our certainty level.
LLMs, on the other hand, are essentially stuck in System 1. They generate responses by predicting the most likely next word based on patterns in their training data. There’s no deliberate reflection, no stepping back to assess confidence levels.
But Wait—What About Reasoning Models? Here’s where things get really interesting, and frankly, concerning. You’d think that reasoning models like OpenAI’s o1 and o3—the ones that can engage in “System 2” thinking—would be better at saying “I don’t know,” right?
They’re actually worse.
According to OpenAI’s own internal testing, their newer reasoning models hallucinate more frequently than their predecessors:3
o1: 16% hallucination rate on PersonQA benchmark o3: 33% hallucination rate (roughly double) o4-mini: 48% hallucination rate For comparison, the non-reasoning GPT-4o had a 30% hallucination rate, while GPT-4.5 achieved 19%.
This completely breaks the historical trend where each new model incrementally hallucinated less than the previous one. OpenAI admits they don’t really know why this is happening, writing in their technical report that “more research is needed” to understand why hallucinations are getting worse as they scale up reasoning models.
The working theory? The reinforcement learning used for reasoning models may amplify issues that are usually mitigated by standard training pipelines. Because these models generate more detailed responses, they make “more accurate claims as well as more inaccurate/hallucinated claims.”
It’s like giving someone more time to think makes them more confident in both their correct and incorrect answers.
The Training Data Problem Here’s where it gets really interesting. LLMs struggle with “I don’t know” partly because of how they’re trained. Think about it: when you’re browsing the internet (where most training data comes from), you either find information about a topic or you don’t. People rarely write “I don’t know” about things they don’t know—they just don’t write about them at all.
So LLMs rarely see examples of confident uncertainty in their training data. They’re optimized to always generate something, because that’s what their training taught them to do.
The Business Pressure Factor There’s also a more pragmatic reason: user expectations. Companies deploying AI want their models to be helpful. A chatbot that frequently says “I don’t know” might be seen as ineffective. Users often prefer a model that tries to help, even if it occasionally gets things wrong, over one that regularly admits ignorance.
As one researcher put it: “Users will say your model is lazy and doesn’t even try, whereas if you train it to be more likely to produce something that looks like a solution more often, people will think ‘wow, the AI solved this problem I couldn’t solve.’”4
The Metacognitive Gap (And Why Humans Aren’t Perfect Either) But here’s the key difference: humans have metacognitive awareness. We can think about our own thinking. When you ask me about quantum physics, I can reflect on my knowledge and confidently say “I don’t know much about that.” I have a sense of the boundaries of my knowledge.
But let’s be honest—humans make plenty of mistakes too.
Research shows that human error rates are often surprisingly high. In medical diagnosis, primary care doctors misdiagnose about 5% of patients. In journalism, American newspapers had factual errors in 61% of stories. When humans claimed to be 100% certain in knowledge tasks, they were still wrong 20% of the time.5
By comparison, ChatGPT hallucinates about 27% of the time according to 2023 estimates—not dramatically different from human error rates in many domains.
The crucial difference isn’t accuracy—it’s uncertainty acknowledgment.
When Columbia Journalism Review tested ChatGPT on 200 quotes, it falsely attributed 76% of them but only indicated uncertainty in 7 out of 153 cases where it was wrong.6 Humans, despite our overconfidence bias, still retain the capacity to say “I don’t know” when we recognize we’re at the limits of our knowledge.
LLMs don’t have this self-awareness. They can’t step back and assess their own knowledge state. They’re pattern-matching machines that generate the most statistically likely next word based on their training, without any real understanding of what they do or don’t “know.”
The goal isn’t perfection—it’s building AI systems that can acknowledge their limitations as humans naturally do, even if imperfectly.
What Can We Muggles Do About It? So here we are: reasoning models that hallucinate more than their predecessors, training data that rarely includes “I don’t know,” and business pressures that reward confident responses over cautious ones.
Sounds hopeless? It’s not. While we can’t fix the underlying architecture, we can dramatically improve our interactions with these systems through better prompting techniques. Think of it as context engineering for uncertainty management.
1. “According to…” Prompting This is probably the easiest and most effective technique. Instead of asking “What causes climate change?” try “According to scientific consensus, what causes climate change?”
This guides the model to ground its response in specific sources rather than generating from general training patterns. It’s like giving the model a specific knowledge base to draw from rather than asking it to freestyle.
Example:
❌ “How do vaccines work?” ✅ “According to medical literature, how do vaccines work?” 2. Progressive Prompting Start broad, then narrow down. This helps you identify when the model is moving from confident territory into speculation.7
Example:
First: “What do you know about renewable energy policy?” Then: “What specific policies were implemented in Germany in 2023?” Finally: “What was the exact impact on household electricity costs?” Watch for the point where responses become vague or overly general—that’s often where hallucination risk increases.
3. Role-Based Prompting Ask the AI to respond as a specific expert who would naturally acknowledge limitations.
Example:
❌ “Explain this medical condition.” ✅ “As a medical researcher, explain this condition, including what aspects are well-understood and what remains uncertain.” 4. Set Output Constraints Shorter, more focused answers reduce the chances of drift into hallucination territory.
Example:
❌ “Tell me everything about artificial intelligence.” ✅ “In 100 words, explain the main types of machine learning.” 5. The 3-6 Second Rule (Applied to AI) Remember that 3-6 second pause I developed for human communication? It works for AI too. Before hitting send, pause and ask yourself:
Am I providing enough context for this request? Could this question be interpreted in multiple ways? Am I asking for information that might not exist or be verifiable? This connects directly to the context engineering insights from my previous post—better context leads to better responses, whether you’re “prompting” humans or machines.
Enterprise Implications: When Stakes Are Higher While these prompting techniques help individual users, enterprises dealing with customer support, financial research, or technical documentation need more systematic approaches. This is where architectural solutions become crucial.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): The Double-Edged Sword I’ll admit, I’m usually skeptical when people immediately jump to RAG as the solution for everything. But for hallucination reduction, it’s actually one of the most effective approaches we have.
RAG works by giving the model access to specific, verified information sources before it generates a response. Instead of relying purely on training data, the model can “look up” relevant information and ground its responses in those sources.
The results are significant: A 2024 Stanford study found that combining RAG with other techniques led to a 96% reduction in hallucinations compared to baseline models. In healthcare, RAG-powered tools reduced diagnostic errors by 15%.8
But there’s a catch: “hallucination with citations.” Models can still confidently generate incorrect responses while citing real sources that don’t actually support their claims. It’s like having a research assistant who finds the right papers but misunderstands what they say.
Grounding and Attribution Technologies This is where newer approaches like Contextual AI’s “groundedness” technology become interesting. Instead of just retrieving information, these systems are designed to “stick to the knowledge sources you give them.”9
Key features include:
Inline attributions: Source citations integrated directly into responses Faithfulness prioritization: Prioritizing retrieved knowledge over training data Controllable groundedness: Settings to manage how strictly the model adheres to sources Think of it as the difference between a research assistant who paraphrases everything in their own words versus one who quotes directly from sources and tells you exactly where each piece of information came from.
The Enterprise Trade-off For enterprises, the calculation is different than for individual users. When a hallucination could mean misrepresenting company policy to customers or providing incorrect financial advice, the cost of verification becomes worth it.
But these solutions aren’t magic bullets. They require:
High-quality data sources (garbage in, garbage out) Robust data governance (who maintains the knowledge base?) Clear attribution chains (can we trace claims back to sources?) Regular auditing (are our sources current and accurate?) The enterprise lesson? Reducing hallucinations isn’t just about better prompting—it’s about building systems that can reliably distinguish between what they know and what they’re guessing.
The Bigger Picture Understanding hallucination mechanisms doesn’t just make us better at using AI—it makes us better at recognizing our own cognitive limitations. When I catch myself confidently stating something I’m not sure about, I think of Claude’s misfiring circuits. When I see a colleague jumping to conclusions without enough context, I think about System 1 vs. System 2 thinking.
The goal isn’t to eliminate uncertainty—it’s to become more conscious about when we’re operating in uncertain territory, whether we’re human or machine.
So why can’t LLMs say “I don’t know”? Because they’re designed to always generate something, trained on data that rarely models uncertainty, and rewarded for helpfulness over accuracy. But more importantly, they lack the metacognitive awareness that allows humans to recognize the boundaries of their knowledge.
The solution isn’t waiting for perfect AI. It’s becoming better context engineers—for both humans and machines.
Back in that POC meeting, when my tech lead mentioned hallucination concerns, we were right to take them seriously. But now I understand that “setting expectations with users” isn’t just about disclaimers—it’s about building systems and processes that acknowledge uncertainty as a feature, not a bug.
Whether we’re implementing RAG systems, training users on better prompting techniques, or just having more honest conversations about AI limitations, the path forward requires the same conscious effort I committed to in my first blog post.
The conscious effort to think deliberately about where the boundaries of knowledge lie—and to say “I don’t know” when we’re crossing them.
