The Fear Was Right, But Not For The Reason I Expected Three months ago, I wrote about my fear of losing the ability to think independently in an age of AI automation. I was worried about the urge to just hit “tab, tab, tab” and accept every autocompletion without conscious thought. Looking back now, that fear was prophetic—but not in the way I expected.
The past three months have been a whirlwind of AI developments. GPT-5 was announced for summer 2025, Google released Imagen 4, Claude got integrations, and the AI market is projected to grow from $189 billion to $4.8 trillion by 2033. The acceleration is real, and it’s happening faster than anyone predicted.
But here’s what I discovered: the bottleneck was never where I thought it was.
The Real Bottleneck: Context, Not Code A blog post that resonated deeply with me during this period was “Writing Code Was Never The Bottleneck”. The author argues that software development’s true constraints have always been human-centric: code reviews, knowledge transfer, testing, debugging, and coordination. While AI tools make code generation faster, they don’t solve the fundamental challenges of understanding, reviewing, and maintaining code.
This insight extends far beyond software development. It’s about where value actually lives in knowledge work.
Think about consulting firms. They don’t charge $500/hour because they can analyze data faster than their clients. They get paid because they can translate complex problems into executive-digestible insights. The bottleneck isn’t the analysis—it’s the communication, stakeholder management, and organizational change.
My Accidental Discovery: Context Engineering For Humans As a Senior Product Manager, my role involves constant context management. Surprisingly, AI didn’t replace my thinking—it taught me to get better at “prompting humans.”
I’ve developed a habit of holding off 3-6 seconds before I speak. During that pause, I:
Line up my ask against their previous conversation Check if I’m missing any facts that could cause confusion Ensure I have enough context to make my request clear I realized I was applying LLM principles to human communication. In LLMs, missing context causes hallucination. In humans, it causes misunderstanding, frustration, and decision paralysis.
That 3-6 second pause became my “context validation layer” before human interaction.
The Industry Catches Up: Context Engineering is The New Trend Just as I was discovering this personally, the AI industry began shifting from “prompt engineering” to “context engineering.” According to recent trends in 2025:
Context engineering is being defined as “building dynamic systems to provide the right information and tools in the right format such that the LLM can plausibly accomplish the task”1 Andrej Karpathy describes it as: “Context engineering is the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step”2 Shopify CEO Tobi Lutke calls it “the art of providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM”3 The insight that’s driving this shift? Most agent performance issues stem from inadequate context, not model limitations. Context engineering addresses failures when agents are missing critical contextual information, have poorly formatted context, or lack appropriate tools.1
The Pattern Recognition The parallels are striking:
Software development: The bottleneck isn’t writing code, it’s context—understanding, reviewing, coordinating Consulting: The bottleneck isn’t analysis, it’s context—translating insights for decision-makers AI systems: The bottleneck isn’t the model, it’s context—providing the right information at the right time Product management: The bottleneck isn’t having ideas, it’s context—aligning stakeholders and managing information flow What This Means Going Forward My original fear about “tab, tab, tab” automation was valid, but I was worried about the wrong thing. The real risk isn’t that AI will make me lazy at the easy parts—it’s that by automating the “easy” parts, the human parts become exponentially more valuable.
The 3-6 second rule isn’t just a communication technique; it’s a form of conscious effort applied where it actually matters. Instead of fighting AI tools, I’m learning to be more deliberate about context management—whether that’s with humans, systems, or AI agents.
As the industry moves toward context engineering, I realize I’ve been inadvertently training for this shift. Product managers are natural context engineers. We spend our days managing information flow, translating between stakeholders, and ensuring everyone has the right context to make good decisions.
The Irony Here’s the beautiful irony: I feared AI would make me think less. Instead, it taught me to think more deliberately about the parts that actually matter. The conscious effort I committed to isn’t about resisting automation—it’s about focusing human intelligence where it creates the most value.
The flying wheel I wrote about three months ago—providing context to get better answers, then asking for clarification to provide better context—isn’t just how you prompt AI effectively. It’s how you build successful products, lead teams, and create value in an automated world.
The bottleneck was never the code. It was never the analysis. It was never the prompt.
The bottleneck is context. It always has been.
And that’s exactly where humans excel—if we choose to think consciously about it.

OpenAI GPT4o generate image with Ghibli style Why I’m setting this blog up partly as a journal. AI makes many things easier: coding, automation, summaries, learning new skills. It’s a blessing AI is developing now, with promising outlooks ahead. But with all the upsides, I fear losing my ability to think for myself. I feel the urge to just hit ’tab’, ’tab’, ’tab’ and accept every autocompletion. I’m not sure if I agree with the autocompletion, but I was willing to trade for the convenience. Scary! It’s a laziness I need to fight. Like tearing down muscle to get bigger, or sticking to a running routine to prep for Marathon. Our bodies are built to save energy, but that won’t get us where we want to go. If resting in peace is the ultimate goal, there’s no point doing anything. So, I need some prove to myself that I did put in the conscious effort.
Another reason for this, is that I want to get better at communication. More specifically, I want to get better at “prompting”, both against LLM and human. Even a tiny LLM models nowadays contain unimaginable amount of knowledge, that means everyone can get an good educated answer if they have a well defined question. If answering becomes so cheap, asking the right questions will become the key to solve problems. And asking good questions comprise two key components IMO, including enough context and asking for clarification. It sort of works like a flying wheel. By providing enought context, I can get answer closer to what I want. And by asking for clarification, I can provide answer closer to what was desired. If we do this right, both LLM or human can having meaningful conversation within 3 shot prompting.
What I consume a lot of information about AI – from technical papers on new model architectures and training techniques to news articles about industry trends, video explainers, and insightful Twitter threads. My interests range from large language models to ethical AI development and practical applications. While I sometimes share interesting finds on LinkedIn, the platform often feels geared towards professional achievements rather than personal learning journeys, which can feel a bit cringy for sharing raw thoughts or works-in-progress. So, this blog will be my space for that. Expect to see summaries of papers I found impactful, reflections on AI news, perhaps collections of useful links with my commentary (archiving my learning path, so to speak), and maybe even attempts at explaining complex concepts simply. I want this to be a place for genuine exploration, not just polished results.
How Just like training for a marathon, consistency comes from enjoyment. My goal isn’t just to write, but to enjoy the process of thinking, articulating, and sharing. How? By focusing on topics that genuinely excite me, setting a sustainable rhythm (maybe one post a week?), and hopefully, engaging with any readers who might find this interesting. As I was writing this, I had a thought about YouTubers constantly asking for engagement – ‘Like, Subscribe, hit the bell!’ It struck me that maybe they genuinely mean it. As social creatures, perhaps we’re wired to thrive on positive connection and feedback. Sharing publicly feels vulnerable, though. Putting thoughts out there invites commentary, and not all of it might be positive. Am I ready to deal with potential criticism or misunderstanding? I’m not entirely sure, but the desire to document my learning and connect outweighs the fear for now. I plan to moderate comments and focus on constructive interaction. This blog is primarily for my own growth, but if others find value or want to discuss these topics, that would make the effort even more rewarding.
Conclusion So, this is the start.(How interesting to start conclusion section saying it’s the start!) A space carved out for deliberate thought in an age of automation, a commitment to clearer communication, and a public log of my ongoing learning journey, particularly around AI. It’s an experiment in progress. Whether you’re here for the AI insights, the reflections on learning, or just to see how this unfolds, I’m glad to have you along for the ride. Let’s see where this conscious effort takes us.
